units.title: Basic Characteristics of the Indian Economy; Planning since Independence; NITI Aayog; Growth and Distributive Justice; HDI; Environmental Degradation; Sustainable Development

rows.title: Basic characteristics of the Indian economy; features of a developing economy
sub: Group-II M2-A-1: Structure of the Indian economy - basic characteristics and sectoral composition

secs.t: Causes of underdevelopment - list of causes and the most fundamental

x: All four statements correctly describe recorded causes of underdevelopment: inadequate savings, population pressure, disguised unemployment and weak human capital indicators.
Ragnar Nurkse's vicious circle is low income leading to low saving, low investment and low productivity, which in turn leads back to low income.
Basic and capital goods accounted for only about
one-fourth
of industrial production at Independence, indicating India's weak industrial base.

secs.t: Mixed economy - definition, vs joint sector, capitalism, controlled economy

x: The State regulates the private sector in a mixed economy through instruments such as taxation, subsidies and credit.
India's middle path retained State control over the commanding heights, particularly
heavy industry, infrastructure and finance
, while permitting a regulated private sector in consumer goods.
Although India has both public and
private sector
s, the largest share of national income is attributed to the private sector in this classification.

secs.t: Features of an underdeveloped/developing economy - statement checks

x: Exam angle: statements matching a feature (regulation through taxes/credit, coexistence of sectors) to the correct label.
Underdeveloped economies are characterised by low per capita income, low capital formation, agricultural predominance and disguised unemployment, not high and uniformly distributed income.

Mixed economy matches public-private coexistence; developing economy matches the infrastructure precondition; underdeveloped economy matches its structural deficiencies; dual economy matches the coexistence of modern and traditional sectors.

secs.t: Types of economies - capitalist, socialist, Gandhian, mixed

x: A capitalist economy is characterised by private ownership, the profit motive and market prices.
India, the United Kingdom and
Germany
are cited as examples of mixed economies, where public and private sectors coexist.
India follows a mixed-economy approach that is described as a pragmatic middle path between
liberal-capitalist, Soviet and Gandhian models

secs.t: Dual economy - organised vs unorganised, rural vs urban divide

x: The organised sector is formal, regulated and associated with social security.
Rural work was dominated by agriculture at 57.7% and self-employment at 62.8%.
Urban work was dominated by services at 62.0% and regular wage or salaried jobs at 49.8%.
Lewis's dual-sector model describes surplus labour moving from
the subsistence sector to the modern sector

secs.t: India's world standing - GDP rank (nominal, PPP), World Bank income class

x: Exam angle: nominal vs PPP rank; which method and which variable (GNI, not GDP) the World Bank uses.
The IMF World Economic Outlook of April 2026 placed India
sixth
in nominal GDP, at USD 4.15 trillion.
The World Bank revises its income groups every
1 July
, using GNI per capita calculated by the Atlas method.

secs.t: AP economy profile - agriculture share of GSDP, per capita income vs India

x: The AP Budget 2026-27 quoted 2024-25 shares of 37% for agriculture, 21% for manufacturing or industry and 42% for services.
The budget quoted Andhra Pradesh's per capita GSDP as Rs 2,98,058 and India's per capita GDP as Rs 2,34,859.
Per capita GSDP is a gross measure, whereas per capita income is calculated as NSDP divided by population.

secs.t: Activities → sector - primary, secondary, tertiary, real sector

x: Exam angle: match codes asked in G1 2022 and 2023 - Trade = Service, Water supply = Industrial, Fisheries = Primary, GDP = CSO; "tertiary sector is also called service sector"; transport is tertiary, not mining/fishing/cement.
Mining and quarrying are primary activities in the activity-based classification but may be counted within the broad Industry sector in the three-sector presentation.

secs.t: Ownership structure - public, private, joint and cooperative sectors

x: National accounts compile GVA separately for general government, public corporations, private corporations and households.
Private corporate investment declined to
11.2 per cent
of GDP in FY24 from 12.3 per cent in FY23.
The private corporate share of Gross Fixed Capital Formation stood at
33 per cent
, its lowest level in a decade.

secs.t: Sectoral composition shift - share in GDP vs share in employment

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason on "structural change in the composition of national income" - both true, R explains A.
tertiary sector
accounted for 52.9 per cent, compared with 21.4 per cent for the primary sector and 25.8 per cent for the secondary sector.
Changes in sectoral output shares, alongside the continuing concentration of employment in agriculture, demonstrate structural change in the economy.

secs.t: Demographic features - population size, dependency ratio, dividend window

x: A TFR of 1.9 is
below the replacement level of 2.1
, indicating that fertility has fallen below the level required for long-term population replacement.
Median age rose from 24 in 2011 to about 29 and is projected to reach 36 by 2036.
The dependency ratio is expected to decline from about
over the decade.

secs.t: Rural-urban structure and regional imbalance indicators

x: Higher work participation in these States is associated with subsistence work and the need for manual labour, especially in rural activities.
Per capita income differences, poverty ratios and variations in sectoral composition are all indicators of regional imbalance.
Telangana’s per capita income was reported to be
1.35 times
that of Andhra Pradesh in 2024-25.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The cited criticism highlights the coexistence of a large GDP with an HDI rank of 130, indicating that economic size does not automatically ensure equivalent human development.
All three figures are reported Andhra Pradesh indicators: 11.3 per cent GSDP growth over 2024-26, per capita income of Rs 2,94,507 in 2025-26, and projected per capita GSDP of Rs 2,98,058.

rows.title: Structural change - sectoral composition of output and employment; the missing manufacturing transition
sub: Group-II M2-A-6: Sectoral distribution of income in India - shares of agriculture, industry and services

secs.t: Sector classification - activity to sector, alternative names

x: The Quinary sector consists of top decision-making activities such as government policy, scientific research and health or education administration.

The new-series revisions reported increases of 7.8–9.0% for finance, real estate and professional services, a 23–26% decline for trade and transport/storage, and a 5.7% rise for hotels and restaurants.
Mining and quarrying are grouped under the primary sector, water supply under the secondary or industrial sector, and transport and storage under the tertiary sector.

secs.t: Sectoral share of employment vs share of output - the mismatch

x: The
Secondary sector
contributed 24.29% of GDP and accounted for 22.24% of the workforce in 2021-22.
The Primary sector employed 43.96% of the workforce but contributed 21.82% of GDP.
A structural change in the composition of national income has occurred, reflected in the changing relative importance of the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.

secs.t: Services-led growth - post-1991 growth driver, premature deindustrialisation

x: Services often require high skills and may not absorb semi-skilled workers leaving agriculture, contributing to jobless growth.
“Premature leapfrogging” describes services absorbing value while manufacturing fails to absorb surplus labour released from farming.

Both statements are true, and the manufacturing sector's linkages with logistics, IT and finance, together with its stabilising effect on GDP cycles, explain why it is considered necessary for sustainable service-led growth.

secs.t: Sectoral share of GVA over time - agriculture, industry, services

x: Exam angle: the 2024-25 "primary" share (21.4%) includes mining, so it is not directly comparable with the old "agriculture, forestry & fishing" share.
The new series reports manufacturing at 14.7 percent, although its absolute size is approximately
1.5-1.6 percent smaller
The Economic Survey explains that the decline in manufacturing's nominal share reflects
a relative-price effect
; in real terms, it remains stable at 17-18 percent.
The 2024-25 primary-sector figure includes mining, whereas the older agriculture-related measure referred to agriculture, forestry and fishing.

secs.t: Clark-Fisher / Lewis model of structural transformation

x: The Clark-Fisher model predicts a transition from the primary sector to the secondary sector and then to the tertiary sector as income rises.
The Lewis turning point is reached when the surplus labour available for transfer from agriculture to the modern sector is exhausted.
India has experienced a service-led shift in output while labour transfer from agriculture has been slow; approximately 46 percent of workers remain in agriculture.

secs.t: AP sectoral composition of GSVA vs India

x: In 2023-24, agriculture and allied activities contributed 37 percent, industry 23 percent and services 40 percent of AP's GSVA.
Fishing and aquaculture
recorded the highest growth within the agriculture and allied sector, at 17.69 percent.
Andhra Pradesh is moving from farming towards services without passing through a strong manufacturing stage, a pattern described as a missing manufacturing transition.

secs.t: Institutions compiling sectoral income - matching body to data

x: GDP and sectoral GVA are compiled by the Central Statistical Organisation, now the National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
GDP and sectoral GVA are compiled by the NSO; State GSDP and sectoral GVA by the State DES; and ASI and ASUSE manufacturing components by the NSO.
Manufacturing GVA was estimated at Rs 38.6 lakh crore, equivalent to
14.7 percent
of GDP in 2023-24 under the new NAS.

secs.t: Sectoral growth rates vs sectoral shares

x: Agriculture recorded real growth of
in 2025-26 according to the sectoral growth table.
The chronological sequence is 2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26 and Q1 2026-27, giving
B, D, A, C
A sector growing more slowly than GDP tends to lose its share in GDP, although its absolute output may still increase.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Telangana's services sector increased from 1.25 times AP's level in 2013-14 to 1.47 times in 2024-25.
Growth was led by finance, real estate, IT and professional services at 12.1%; the secondary sector grew by 8.6%.
The rounded Budget 2026-27 presentation gives
agriculture 37%, industry 21% and services 42%
The cited Group-II 2017 key used the split of
31.77% agriculture, 22.23% industry and 46.0% services

rows.title: Services sector - growth, composition and contribution to GDP and employment
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I C-2

secs.t: Services share in GVA and in employment - trend and mismatch

x: Exam angle: services' contribution to GDP is "more than 50%"; to employment "about a third".
The tertiary sector accounted for 53.89% of GDP, while the primary sector employed 43.96% of the workforce.
The
tertiary sector
recorded the greatest rise in employment share, although the movement of output away from agriculture was faster than the movement of employment.

secs.t: Service-led growth model - post-1991 growth driver, sustainability debate

x: The services boom began in the mid-1980s and gained speed following the economic reforms of the 1990s.
All three statements are correct: manufacturing employed about 72 million persons, while services are characterised as a high-growth, low-volatility anchor growing at roughly 7–8% annually.

secs.t: Services exports - software, business services, India's share and targets

x: Using WTO data, the India Year Book 2026 ranks India
eighth
in global services exports, with a 4.3% share.
India's services exports were USD 387.5 billion and imports were USD 198.7 billion in 2024-25, resulting in a surplus.
All three statements are correct: growth was 15.3% in FY2025-26, the FY2023-FY2025 CAGR was 14%, and this was approximately twice the pre-pandemic 7.6% rate.

secs.t: Composition - tertiary activities vs primary and secondary

x: Trade, hotels and restaurants, public administration and defence are tertiary activities, while manufacturing, construction and utilities are secondary.
International bodies such as the WTO use
the United Nations Central Product Classification
, or UNCPC, for services.
The income method is used for service activities such as trade, transport, banking, real estate, public administration and other services.

secs.t: Services PMI and high-frequency indicators

x: The ISP is a fixed-weight Laspeyres volume index with weights based on GVA.
The ISP draws data from
GST returns and administrative records
MoSPI's Index of Services Production is the services counterpart of the IIP; its stated base is 2024-25 and it covers 19 sub-sectors representing about 60% of services.

secs.t: Global capability centres (GCCs)

x: A GCC is an offshore unit set up by a multinational to undertake its own core work, unlike a third-party vendor.
NASSCOM reported 1,760 GCCs employing about 19 lakh persons in FY2025.
The number of GCCs has risen to over 1,800, and their foreign-exchange-generating activities help cushion the merchandise trade deficit.

secs.t: GATS modes of supply

x: Mode 2 is consumption abroad, illustrated by a person travelling overseas for medical treatment.
Mode 3 refers to commercial presence, including a foreign branch or subsidiary established in the country where the service is supplied.
Mode 4 concerns the temporary presence of natural persons, such as IT professionals working in another country on visas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct for 2025-26: services GVA was Rs 3,59,931 crore, growth was 10.67%, and communications grew fastest at 15.13%.
Karnataka, along with Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Telangana, produces about 40% of India's services output; 58.7% is the figure associated with Bihar's GSVA share from services.
Kerala's and Bihar's services shares are 64.3% and 58.7%, respectively, and the activity is characterised as mostly low-value.

rows.title: Role of the IT and ITES industry in India's development - exports, employment and challenges
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I C-2

secs.t: Origins of software exports - Department of Electronics, early policy, STPI

x: The Computer Policy was introduced in 1984 and the Software Export Policy in 1986; the two policies liberalised imports and data links.
STPI has extended its model to smaller
Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
Software exports grew by about
50 percent
annually after 1995–96, aided by low costs and international quality standards.

secs.t: IT-BPM employment - QES, NASSCOM data, rank in job creation

x: NASSCOM estimated about
58 lakh
, or 5.8 million, direct jobs in the IT-BPM industry in FY2025.
IT-BPM employment is mostly in the organised sector and generally involves contracts and social security.
The Labour Bureau's QES tracks employment in nine non-farm sectors, one of which is IT/BPO.
High-end services can record rapid GVA growth but limited employment generation because they are skill-intensive and automated.

secs.t: IT-BPM revenue and exports - growth, forex, largest firms, destinations

x: The figures correspond respectively to FY2021-22, FY2022-23, FY2023-24 and FY2024-25 (estimated): 227, 245, 254 and 283 billion dollars.
Software and computer services are India's largest services export and services forex earner, helping offset the merchandise trade deficit in the balance of payments.
India's IT-BPM exports mainly go to the
USA and Europe
, making the sector sensitive to their visa regimes and client spending cycles.

secs.t: Institutions - NASSCOM, MeitY

x: NASSCOM is the industry body for the IT-BPM sector.
MeitY became a separate ministry in 2016; before that, the department was known as DeitY.
The six goals were e-Government, e-Industry, e-Innovation/R&D, e-Learning, e-Security and e-Inclusion.
e-Agriculture pricing
was not among them.
TIDE 2.0 was launched in 2019 with an allocation of Rs 264.62 crore and 51 incubation centres.

secs.t: IT hubs - major cities and emerging tier-2 centres

x: Seven cities accounted for 70 percent of IT exports, while Bengaluru alone accounted for 38 percent according to the cited CDI data.
Coimbatore, Indore, Jaipur and Bhubaneswar
are identified as emerging Tier-2/Tier-3 centres.
The IT Park at Madhurawada (Rushikonda), Visakhapatnam, is an Andhra Pradesh example under the
AP IT & GCC Policy 4.0

secs.t: Challenges - visa curbs, automation and AI, skill gap

x: Visa rules, protectionism and client spending cycles are all external factors affecting the IT-BPM industry.
Routine ITES/BPM work
is identified as the segment most exposed to automation and generative AI.
The cited NASSCOM-Indeed report identifies cloud, GenAI/LLMs, MLOps and data analytics as important AI-ready skills.
GERD is reported at approximately
0.64–0.7 percent of GDP
in the context of shortages of frontier-AI and chip-design talent.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The concentration of skilled employment in a limited number of cities restricts the industry’s ability to produce broad-based development by itself.
The recent demand for AI-related roles has been led by the banking, financial services and insurance sector and the telecom sector.
STPI, established in 1991, represented
India’s first export-park model for software

rows.title: Other services - tourism, banking, insurance, health and education services
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I C-2

secs.t: Insurance - penetration vs density, IRDAI, private entry, LIC, FDI cap, Insurance for All by 2047

x: The
Malhotra Committee
, constituted in 1993–94, recommended opening insurance to private companies and establishing an independent regulator.
The 2025 amendment raised the FDI cap from 74 per cent to 100 per cent, amended the three specified Acts and created the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund.
Parliament passed the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act on
17 December 2025
; it was notified in late December 2025.

secs.t: Health services - public health expenditure (NHA), Centre + states spending

x: PM-JAY and State schemes together cover about 80 per cent of citizens, but only about 35 per cent of those insured used the benefit.
PM-JAY was launched in 2018 with coverage of Rs 5 lakh per family, and insurance coverage has roughly tripled since its launch.
OOPE declined, social security expenditure increased, and per-capita GHE rose between 2013–14 and 2022–23.

secs.t: Para-banking services - activities permitted to banks

x: Portfolio management and investment advisory, primary dealership and pension fund management are among the permitted para-banking activities.
Banks may undertake insurance business
as a corporate agent or through a joint venture
, subject to the applicable regulatory approval.
Equipment leasing, factoring and mutual-fund business are all among the para-banking activities that banks may undertake with RBI approval.

secs.t: AP health scheme Aarogyasri - launch, eponym, coverage

x: Rajiv Aarogyasri was launched as a cashless health insurance scheme for families below the poverty line and operated through a State trust.
The scheme was named after
Rajiv Gandhi
; it was launched by the Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy government.
State and Central health-insurance schemes together covered approximately
70 per cent
of households in Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Insurance principles and products

x: The principle of indemnity restores the insured to the position existing before the loss and does not permit profit from the insurance claim.
The sovereign-backed P&I cover was launched under the Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool, designed by New India Assurance, issued first to SCI and provided indemnity up to USD 1.5 billion.

secs.t: Education services - public expenditure, NEP 2020 target

x: Education is a subject in the
Concurrent List
, permitting legislative action by both Parliament and State Legislatures subject to constitutional provisions.

secs.t: Transport, postal and telecom - UDAN, post office network, BSNL, tele-density, 5G

x: The post office network supports DBT, Aadhaar services and Postal Life Insurance, whereas regional air connectivity flights are associated with UDAN.
BSNL was corporatised on 1 October 2000, the first UDAN flight took place in April 2017, India Post Payments Bank was launched in 2018, and 5G services began on 1 October 2022.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: More than 40 crore Indians were reported to be in a healthcare gap, while public health spending was reported at 1.43% of GDP.
The IRDAI sub-committee was reviewing
private health insurance
The bank credit-deposit ratio reached
in the first quarter of FY27, described as a 62-year high.
Andhra Pradesh services were reported to be growing at 10.67%, with banking and insurance growing at 13.59%.

rows.title: Occupational structure of India - trends and inter-state variation
sub: Group-II M2-A-5: Occupational pattern in India - trends, structural retardation and informality

secs.t: Occupational structure - share of workforce by sector (Census, NSS, PLFS), highest-employment sector

x: The NSS estimate for 1993-94 placed agriculture's share of workers at
The 2021-22 workforce shares were primary 43.96%, secondary 22.24% and tertiary 33.80%.
The NSSO 70th round reported that
of rural households were agricultural households.
The workforce was reported as 61.6 crore in PLFS 2025, while 56.2 crore were employed in Q2 FY26.

secs.t: Rural vs urban workforce (Census 2011), gender differences

x: The low share of operational holdings held by women, alongside their agricultural work, is associated with the
feminisation of agriculture
Women's earnings were 76% of men's wages in salaried work, 69% in casual work and 36% in self-employment.
PLFS 2025 reported an increase in regular salaried employment from 22% to 24% and a decline in self-employment from 58% to 56%.

secs.t: Trend shifts - cultivators vs agricultural labourers, Census 2001 to 2011

x: Exam angle: direction of change of cultivators vs labourers.
Cultivators declined from 127.3 million to 118.8 million, while agricultural labourers increased from 106.8 million to 144.3 million.
Fragmentation reduced the average holding size and increased the relative importance of small and marginal farmers, contributing to the decline in cultivators.
The average holding size fell to
1.08 hectares
in 2015-16 from 2.28 hectares in 1971.

secs.t: Occupational structure - meaning, and reasons for the slow shift out of agriculture

x: Population pressure on land
helped keep a large workforce dependent on agriculture, so its employment share declined only marginally during the Plan era.
Services-led growth needs appropriate skills, which limits the absorption of surplus agricultural labour into service-sector employment.
Colonial deindustrialisation had already
pushed artisans onto the land
, increasing pressure on agriculture.

secs.t: Inter-state variation - highest/lowest share in agriculture

x: Urbanised Delhi, Chandigarh and Puducherry
have high shares of other workers, including service-sector workers.
Rural women's LFPR gains were led by West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar; urban gains occurred in Rajasthan and Gujarat.

secs.t: AP occupational structure - workforce share in agriculture vs national average

x: AP had a lower cultivator share, 14.5 per cent against 24.7 per cent; a higher all-agriculture share, 62.4 per cent against 54.6 per cent; and a lower other-worker share, 34.8 per cent against 41.6 per cent.
Agriculture
was the largest employer in Andhra Pradesh at 45.6 per cent, followed by services at 31.6 per cent and manufacturing and industry at 22.8 per cent.

secs.t: Jobless growth - meaning, period, reasons

x: Jobless growth denotes GDP or output growth that is not matched by adequate employment growth, especially growth in formal and quality jobs.
In
the late 1990s
, employment growth fell to early-plan levels even while GDP continued to grow.
About
12 million
people enter the Indian job market every year, creating pressure for adequate employment generation.

secs.t: Informal/unorganised employment - features, NCEUS, share, social security

x: The unorganised sector consists largely of small and scattered units outside effective government control, with low pay, little job security and few social benefits.

All three statements are correct: the informal workforce share is about 90 per cent, informal non-farm jobs were about 78 per cent, and short-term or contractual EPFO jobs illustrate formal informality.
Twenty-nine labour laws were merged into four Codes: the Code on Wages in 2019 and the Industrial Relations, Social Security and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Codes in 2020.
NCEUS defined the unorganised sector as unincorporated private enterprises owned by individuals or households, on a proprietary or partnership basis, with fewer than 10 workers.

secs.t: Types of unemployment - sector each is linked with

x: Disguised unemployment
exists when more workers are engaged than necessary and the marginal productivity of some workers is nearly zero.
Seasonal unemployment
arises when work is available only during particular agricultural seasons, especially sowing and harvesting.
Structural unemployment
results from a mismatch between available skills and job requirements caused by technology or broader structural change.

secs.t: Structural retardation - Clark-Fisher thesis

x: The Clark-Fisher thesis describes the progression of labour from primary activities to secondary activities and subsequently to tertiary activities as income increases.

Agriculture's GVA share of about 18% alongside an employment share of 42.4% shows that labour has moved away from agriculture more slowly than output has, a condition described as structural retardation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The United Nations declared 2026 the International Year of the
Woman Farmer
Census 2011 was the 15th Census conducted since 1872 and the 7th Census conducted after Independence.
A fall in unemployment may also reflect distress entry into low-productivity work.
Andhra Pradesh recorded an LFPR of 47.5%, comprising 59.5% for males and 35.8% for females.

rows.title: Economic development since independence - phases and growth rates; the Hindu rate of growth

secs.t: Hindu rate of growth - who coined it, year, variable, period

x: The expression referred to India’s stagnant annual growth during the
The expression referred to annual real GDP growth of approximately 3.5%, or 3.52% for 1950–1980.
Low real GDP growth translated into per capita growth of only about 1.37%, barely above population growth.
India’s growth accelerated to approximately 5.1–5.5% during the 1980s, breaking the earlier stagnant pattern.

secs.t: Policy orientation 1947-1991 - import substitution, licence-permit regime

x: The major policy orientation was import substitution supported by state planning and public investment, rather than export promotion or deregulation.
The Bombay Plan of 1944 was prepared by industrialists who themselves sought state protection, making the Licence Raj partly a capitalist demand.
The 1980s saw a pro-business, not pro-market orientation, including broad-banding of licences, tax cuts, NRI deposits and a higher MRTP limit.

secs.t: Low growth despite high savings - capital-output ratio (ICOR)

x: A lower ICOR means that less additional capital is required to generate one additional unit of output, indicating greater investment efficiency.
Although investment increased from 7% to 11%, capital-intensive industries with long gestation periods resulted in a high ICOR and relatively low growth.
In the Harrod-Domar framework, growth equals the
savings rate divided by the capital-output ratio

secs.t: Chronology of economic milestones and crises

x: Exam angle: arrange these events chronologically.
Rupee devaluation occurred in June 1966, the Green Revolution began in the mid-1960s, bank nationalisation took place in July 1969, and ‘Garibi Hatao’ was launched in 1971.
The wars of 1962 and 1965, along with severe droughts in 1965–66, contributed to the failure of the Third Plan and the Plan Holiday of 1966–69.

secs.t: Phases of Indian development - boundaries and average growth

x: The average annual growth rate during
was approximately 3.5 per cent, or 3.52 per cent.
The average growth rate during 1980–81 to 1989–90 was in the range of 5.13 to 5.18 per cent.
Post-reform growth averaged approximately 6.5 per cent, was 6.8 per cent from 1993–94, and peaked at 8.5 per cent during 2003–08.

secs.t: Turning-point debate - 1980s acceleration vs 1991

x: Dani Rodrik and Arvind Subramanian
argued in 2004 that the growth transition began around 1980 with a pro-business attitudinal shift.
J. Bradford DeLong argued in 2003 that India’s economic take-off occurred in the 1980s, before the 1991 reforms.
The 1980s growth phase is viewed as debt-fuelled and unstable, and it ended in
the 1991 economic crisis

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Job-poor growth and youth unemployment of approximately 10 per cent are identified as important criticisms.
Arvind Subramanian placed India’s growth during 2011–17 at approximately 4.5 per cent, rather than the reported 7 per cent.
The chronological sequence is 13.5 per cent during 2014–19, 10.3 per cent during 2019–24 and 11.3 per cent during 2024–26.

secs.t: Planning Commission vs NDC vs Finance Ministry - who assesses, formulates, approves

x: The Planning Commission assessed resources and prepared the draft plan; the Finance Ministry handled budgetary allocation, while the National Development Council approved the draft as the apex approving body.
The
National Development Council
prescribed guidelines for formulation of the national plan, including assessment of the resources required, and approved the draft plan.

secs.t: National Development Council - year, chairman, secretary, members, functions

x: The Council approved draft Five-Year Plans, linked the Planning Commission with the States and was intended to meet at least twice a year.
A formal resolution for abolishing the National Development Council remains pending, while its role has effectively passed to NITI Aayog's Governing Council.
The National Planning Council constituted in 1965 was
an expert advisory body attached to the Planning Commission

secs.t: Planning and the Constitution - Concurrent List, DPSP, planning machinery

x: The Planning Commission was established in line with the objectives reflected in
Article 39
of the Directive Principles.

The Planning Commission was established in 1950, the National Development Council in 1952, District Planning Committees are covered by Article 243ZD, and Metropolitan Planning Committees by Article 243ZE.
Article 243ZE provides for a Metropolitan Planning Committee for
every metropolitan area
, generally defined in this context as an area with a population of 10 lakh or more.

secs.t: Pre-independence planning efforts - Visvesvaraya, National Planning Committee, other plans

x: The Congress National Planning Committee was initiated by Subhas Chandra Bose, chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, and its final report appeared in 1949.
The Bombay Plan was prepared by eight industrialists, including J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla and Kasturbhai Lalbhai, and sought state-led industrialisation and protection.
The
Gandhian Plan
, prepared by Shriman Narayan Agarwal in 1944, emphasised decentralised and self-contained villages.

secs.t: Epithets for the Planning Commission - 'Economic Cabinet', 'super cabinet'

x: These epithets reflected criticism that the Planning Commission centralised decisions and weakened the autonomy of the States.
The common-plan idea encouraged centralisation and became a continuing source of
Centre-State tension

secs.t: State Planning Boards - AP State Planning Board / AP planning department structure

x: The AP Planning Department brings out the Socio-Economic Survey, monitors Swarna Andhra @2047 and issues Monthly Economic Reports.
Swarna Andhra @2047 monitoring covers 651 key performance indicators across 30 Secretariat departments.
Monitoring is carried out through Vision Monitoring Units at three administrative levels and a Swarna Andhra KPIs dashboard.
The monitoring framework uses a
15% growth target and 651 KPIs in Monthly Economic Reports

secs.t: Decentralised planning - district planning committees, 73rd/74th Amendment link

x: The
Balwantrai Mehta Committee
recommended in 1957 that planning and development should be entrusted to Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The Thungon Sub-Committee identified the
Zila Parishad
as the planning pivot at the district level.
Andhra Pradesh introduced district-level decentralised planning during the Sixth Plan (1980–85), allocating Rs 1 crore to each of its 23 districts and setting up District Planning Councils.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The newer approach associated with NITI Aayog emphasises bottom-up planning and cooperative federalism, with a think-tank role rather than fund allocation.
NITI Aayog is described as a think tank that promotes bottom-up planning and cooperative federalism; it is not primarily a fund allocator.

secs.t: Rolling plan - meaning, economist, government, period in force

x: Rolling plans use flexible targets and are revised and extended every year.
The outlay of the rolling plan was Rs.
The rolling plan stressed
employment
in contrast to the emphasis associated with the Nehru model.
Frequent yearly revision was criticised because it weakened commitment to the originally stated targets.

secs.t: Long-term objectives of planning - growth, modernisation, self-reliance, social justice

x: The socialistic pattern of society was adopted at the Avadi Congress in 1955 and was subsequently reflected in the Second Plan and the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956.

The First Plan focused on agriculture, irrigation and power; the Second on rapid industrialisation; the Third on self-reliance and food self-sufficiency; and the Fifth on poverty removal and self-reliance.

secs.t: Imperative vs indicative planning - market mechanism, examples, India's shift

x: Imperative or directive planning replaces the market mechanism with a command hierarchy involving binding decisions and allocations.
India shifted to indicative planning from the Eighth Plan, covering 1992–97, following the economic reforms of 1991.
Indicative planning
uses guidelines, goals and signals to influence private-sector decisions instead of imposing binding quotas.

secs.t: Perspective planning - meaning, time horizon, India's perspective plans

x: Perspective planning was a function of the
Planning Commission
in India.
A long-term perspective plan for 1985–2000 accompanied
the Seventh Plan
Lack of a sufficiently developed perspective has been cited as a standard criticism of Indian planning.
Viksit Bharat @2047, the Swarna Andhra @2047 target of Rs.
DMF five-year perspective plans are prepared using
baseline surveys

secs.t: Planning dichotomies - centralised/decentralised, direction/inducement, financial/physical, democratic/totalitarian

x: Planning by inducement influences behaviour through incentives, including prices, taxes and subsidies.
Financial planning expresses allocation in monetary terms, while physical planning concerns real resources such as materials, manpower and output targets.

India displayed imperative features in the early public sector, moved towards indicative planning and inducement after 1991, and Kerala's People's Plan Campaign is an example of decentralised planning.

secs.t: Multi-level planning - centre, state, district, block, bottom-up goal

x: Multi-level planning operates through NITI Aayog at the Centre, Planning Boards in the States, DPCs at the district level, and block or mandal bodies with Gram Panchayats through GPDPs.

The Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA), Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), Integrated Tribal Development Programme (ITDP) and Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) operated outside the panchayat framework.

secs.t: Planning Commission and NDC - set-up, status, chairman, functions

The Deputy Chairman was the de facto head of the Planning Commission, held Cabinet-minister rank and attended Cabinet meetings without a vote.
The
Unique Identification Authority of India
(UIDAI) was an attached office of the Planning Commission from January 2009.
All four were functions of the Planning Commission: resource assessment, plan formulation, priority-setting, resource allocation, progress appraisal and planning grants to States.
NITI Aayog emphasises bottom-up planning and cooperative federalism and functions primarily as a think tank, not as a fund allocator.
A formal resolution abolishing the National Development Council remains pending; replacement of the Planning Commission did not itself complete that formal abolition.

secs.t: Objectives of planning - chief vs subsidiary

x: Economic growth
is the principal objective of planning, while modernisation, self-reliance and social justice are subsidiary or complementary objectives.
The long-term objectives include growth, modernisation, self-reliance, social justice, employment generation and removal of poverty.
The declared aim combined a rapid rise in living standards with efficient resource use and increased production and employment opportunities for all.

secs.t: Strategy shifts - trickle-down to direct attack on poverty

x: The First to Third Plans followed the
trickle-down approach
, assuming that the benefits of growth would reach poorer sections.
SFDA, MFAL and the Drought Prone Area Programme were listed as programmes under the target-group approach from the Fourth Plan onward.
The Sixth Plan, covering 1980–85, placed removal of poverty foremost and included IRDP, NREP and RLEGP among its programmes.

secs.t: Plan financing - domestic savings, deficit financing, foreign aid

x: Plan expenditure was financed through domestic savings, deficit financing and foreign aid.
Domestic savings for plan financing included budgetary resources, public sector surpluses and market borrowing.
The Harrod-Domar framework links growth to
the savings rate and the capital-output ratio
The
Fourth Plan
aimed to reduce India's dependence on foreign aid.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: NITI Aayog replaced the fixed Five-Year Plan framework with a bottom-up think-tank approach.
NITI Aayog lacks financial powers and represents a shift towards cooperative and competitive federalism rather than centralised plan-grant allocation.
The Viksit Gram Panchayat Plan reflects the contemporary emphasis on
decentralised and perspective-based planning
The new rural employment law is stated to operate on the basis of the
Viksit Gram Panchayat Plan
The Amaravati Economic Region Plan covers nine districts and 44,962 sq km, represents approximately 35.15 percent of GSDP and is one of three economic regions in Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Plan → model it was based on (with distractor model names)

x: The answer is
Harrod-Domar
The Third Five-Year Plan, covering 1961–66, was associated with the
John Sandy and S. Chakravarty model
, known as the Gadgil Yojana model.
The Third Five Year Plan, also known as the Gadgil Yojana, was associated with the John Sandy and S. Chakravarthy growth model and followed an import substitution strategy.
The Feldman-Mahalanobis model focused on the scarcity of capital goods, while the Harrod-Domar model stressed limited aggregate savings.

secs.t: Mahalanobis model - sectors, strategy, omissions, criticisms

x: Consumer goods were largely left to the
small and cottage sector
, while the public sector concentrated on basic and heavy industries.
The Mahalanobis model gave priority to the capital goods sector, including steel and machinery, to build domestic productive capacity.
The model assumed that building machines domestically would eventually enable India to become self-sufficient in producing consumer goods.

secs.t: Non-official plans → author, year, core proposals

x: The Bombay Plan favoured a significant State role, public sector development and protection of infant industries; it did not advocate
a completely non-interventionist State
The Sarvodaya Plan was prepared by Jayaprakash Narayan in 1950 and drew on Gandhian constructive work and Vinoba Bhave’s Sarvodaya ideas.
The Gandhian Plan emphasised agriculture, cottage and village industries, decentralisation, Swadeshi, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship.

secs.t: P.C. Mahalanobis - architect of the Second Plan, institutions founded

x: Mahalanobis helped create the NSSO and CSO, founded the journal Sankhya and devised the Mahalanobis distance.
P.C. Mahalanobis received the Weldon Medal in 1944, became an FRS in 1945 and received the Padma Vibhushan in 1968.
National Statistics Day is observed on 29 June, the birth anniversary of
P.C. Mahalanobis
, since 2007.

secs.t: Harrod-Domar model - capital-output ratio, savings, growth equation

x: The Harrod-Domar model was developed independently by
Roy Harrod and Evsey Domar
The model states that growth depends positively on the savings rate and negatively on the capital-output ratio.
The model links increased investment with higher output and employment through the
multiplier effect

secs.t: Wage-goods model - Vakil and Brahmananda vs Mahalanobis

x: Vakil and Brahmananda put forward the wage-goods model in their 1956 work,
Planning for an Expanding Economy
A larger supply of wage goods makes it possible to support and employ disguised unemployed labour in productive activities.
The wage-goods model favoured agriculture and wage goods, while the Mahalanobis strategy gave priority to heavy industry and capital goods.

secs.t: Janata government alternative strategy - emphasis areas

x: The Janata Party came to power in 1977 while the
Fifth Five Year Plan
was in operation.
The Janata Government ended the Fifth Plan in 1978, adopted a Rolling Plan for 1978–80, and followed a concept advocated by Gunnar Myrdal.
The Janata strategy emphasised agriculture, rural development, employment, small and cottage industries, and minimum needs rather than heavy industry.

x: The Governing Council comprises the Prime Minister, all State Chief Ministers, Chief Ministers of Union Territories with legislatures, and Lieutenant Governors of the remaining Union Territories, along with specified NITI Aayog members and invitees.
The 11th Governing Council meeting was held under the theme “
Inclusive Human Development for Viksit Bharat@2047

secs.t: NITI Aayog vs Planning Commission

x: All four statements correctly describe the institutional differences: the Planning Commission used the usual process for its Member-Secretary and had no part-time members, while NITI Aayog’s CEO is appointed by the Prime Minister and part-time members may be included as needed.

The Planning Commission limited the role of States largely to the National Development Council and annual plan discussions, whereas NITI Aayog gives every Chief Minister a direct role through its Governing Council.

secs.t: AP engagement with NITI Aayog

x: Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu presented
Swarna Andhra @2047
at the 11th Governing Council meeting on 11 June 2026.
Swarna Andhra @2047 focuses on zero poverty, jobs and a human-capital-driven, globally competitive economy.
Chief Minister
N. Chandrababu Naidu
convened the Swachh Bharat sub-group and presented Swarna Andhra @2047 to NITI Aayog.

secs.t: Objectives in the Cabinet resolution

x: NITI Aayog’s stated functions include partnerships with think tanks, support for knowledge, innovation and entrepreneurship, and monitoring and evaluation.
NITI Aayog follows a bottom-up approach and cooperative, or “marble-cake”, federalism, along with Antyodaya and inclusive and participatory development.
Antyodaya, inclusive and participatory development, and attention to small enterprises are guiding priorities.

In 2016, NITI Aayog was asked to prepare a Fifteen-Year Vision, a Seven-Year Strategy and a Three-Year Action Agenda to replace the Five-Year Plans.
State Vision@2047 documents are aligned with the national framework of
Viksit Bharat @2047

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, are chaired by the Union Home Minister, and a NITI Aayog representative attends as an adviser.
NITI Aayog signifies a move away from the top-down Planning Commission model towards collaborative partnership with States.
NITI Aayog’s State rankings encourage
competitive federalism
by comparing performance across States and promoting improvement.

4th
, SDG-7
1st

2nd
for 2020-21. For 2023-24 remember
9th
, with SDG-7 and SDG-14 unchanged.
The 2023-24 edition uses 113 MoSPI-aligned indicators, scores 16 goals quantitatively with a composite score, and assesses SDG 17 qualitatively.
The categories are Achiever at 100, Front Runner from 65 to 99, Performer from 50 to 64, and Aspirant below 50.
Andhra Pradesh’s score rose from 72 to 74, but its rank fell from fourth to ninth; a score of 74 places it in the Front Runner band.

N. Chandrababu Naidu
NITI Aayog
uses the SDG India Index as its main tool for localising the Sustainable Development Goals and encouraging competitive federalism.
Andhra Pradesh recorded a score of 74, was classified as a Front Runner and stood 9th according to the stated APSES presentation.

secs.t: Index → publisher

x: The Sustainable Development Report or SDG Index is published by the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN), not NITI Aayog.

The VNR is prepared by UN Member States; the NER District SDG Index is associated with NITI Aayog and MoDoNER with UNDP support; the SDG Urban Index is by NITI Aayog; and the SDG-NIF Progress Report is by MoSPI.
The Sustainable Development Report 2025 placed India 99th out of 167 countries, with a score of approximately 67, marking India’s first entry into the top 100.
MoSPI monitors progress through the NIF, which had 277 indicators in 2026, while NITI Aayog leads SDG localisation.

secs.t: State rankings → top state, AP position

x: India ranked 38th out of
139 countries
in 2025, improving from 81st position in 2015.
NITI Aayog publishes the Composite Water Management, Export Preparedness and School Education Quality indices, and also undertakes Water Budgeting in Aspirational Blocks.
Odisha ranked first among major States for the second year running, Punjab was last, and Arunachal Pradesh led the North-Eastern and Himalayan States.

secs.t: SDG India Index categories and nodal body

x: The remaining category, Performer, covers scores from 50 to 64.
MoSPI frames the National Indicator Framework, while NITI Aayog oversees the SDGs.

x: Strategy for New India @75 was released in 2018.
The framework introduced in 2016 consists of a 15-year Vision, a 7-year Strategy and a 3-year Action Agenda.
Under the State Support Mission, States prepare
State Vision@2047
documents in line with Viksit Bharat @2047.
Swarna Andhra @2047 is Andhra Pradesh’s State Vision@2047 document aligned with
Viksit Bharat @2047

x: NITI indices make competitive federalism measurable and help convert national goals into district-level outcomes.
The index assigns 50% to transport electrification, 30% to charging infrastructure and 20% to EV research and innovation.
National multidimensional poverty fell from 55.3% in 2005-06 to 14.96% in 2019-21 and was estimated at 11.28% in 2022-23.

rows.title: Economic growth vs economic development; measures of development
sub: Group-II M2-A-7: Economic growth and economic development - concepts, measures and indicators

secs.t: Development theories → proponent

x: Ragnar Nurkse
is associated with the vicious circle of poverty, expressed through the idea that a country is poor because it remains poor.
Albert O. Hirschman discussed unbalanced growth in
The Strategy of Economic Development
, published in 1958.
Rostow’s sequence is traditional society, pre-conditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity and age of high mass consumption.

secs.t: Growth vs development - basis of distinction

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT emphasised by the new view" - answer is the simple growth rate only.
Real GDP or real GNP
measures changes in output and is therefore a conventional measure of economic growth.
The term
sustainable growth
is used for a policy aim directed towards the economic and social well-being of people.
Growth is regarded as a means, whereas development is the broader end involving improved well-being, capabilities and distribution.
The Western model places economic growth, rising GDP and industrialisation at the centre of development.

secs.t: Models of development - Western model vs welfare-centred alternatives

x: The Gandhian model, Kerala model and capability approach are welfare-centred alternatives.
The Gandhian model emphasises decentralisation and village industry.
The Directive Principles envisage adequate livelihood and reduced inequality, rather than merely a higher national income.

secs.t: Indicators of economic development - structural and institutional change

x: A larger share of GDP from the primary sector is not treated as an indicator of economic development.
Human resource development is an important sign and component of economic development.
Structural transformation involves movement from an agrarian economy towards industrial and service sectors.

secs.t: New view of development - poverty, unemployment, inequality

x: The new view defines development in terms of falling poverty, unemployment and inequality within a growing economy, rather than growth alone.
Dudley Seers
is associated with the new view of development and wrote The Meaning of Development in 1969.
An increase in per-capita GNP may indicate economic growth, but it does not signify development if poverty and unemployment are increasing.

secs.t: Measures of development - PCI, PQLI, HDI, GNH

x: The HDI was developed by Mahbub ul Haq with the contribution of
Amartya Sen
Paul Samuelson is associated with NEW, Nordhaus and Tobin with MEW, and Corrado Gini with the Gini coefficient.
Gross National Happiness was introduced as an idea by
Bhutan's fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck
, during the 1970s.
Bhutan
adopted Gross National Happiness, emphasizing well-being domains rather than relying exclusively on GNP.
The team that led the first Human Development Report in 1990 was led by
Mahbub ul Haq and Inge Kaul

secs.t: Development classics → author

x: Gunnar Myrdal wrote Economic Theory and Underdeveloped Regions; A.O. Hirschman wrote The Strategy of Economic Development; Charles P. Kindleberger wrote Strategic Factors in Economic Development.
The Strategy of Economic Development, published in 1958, was written by
A.O. Hirschman
Economic Theory and Underdeveloped Regions was written by
Gunnar Myrdal

secs.t: Capital-output ratio and savings-investment rate as growth determinants

x: Idle or poorly used capital, absence of complementary inputs, and inadequate demand can all prevent capital formation from raising output.
Capital-intensive investment relies relatively more on capital and may therefore generate limited employment compared with labour-intensive investment.

secs.t: Growth terms → who coined and what it described

x: Exam angle: "Who used the term Hindu rate of growth and why" - Raj Krishna, stagnant growth.
Trickle-down is the belief that the benefits of growth will percolate automatically to poorer sections of society.
The stated concern is that approximately
50 per cent
of rural people cannot afford two thali meals a day.

secs.t: Curves → relationship shown

x: The Kuznets curve presents an inverted-U relationship: inequality initially rises and subsequently falls with increasing income.
The Environmental Kuznets Curve suggests that pollution initially rises and later falls as per capita income increases.
The Laffer curve shows that tax revenue may decline when tax rates are increased beyond a certain point.

secs.t: Determinants of growth - economic vs non-economic factors

x: Capital formation through savings and investment is an economic determinant of growth.
Natural resources and technical progress are economic factors, while effective institutions, rule of law, population quality and social structure are non-economic factors.
The public capital expenditure allocation of ₹11.11 lakh crore generated output of approximately four times its value and also crowded in private capital.

secs.t: Sustainable development - Brundtland, green GDP, green economy

x: A green economy is low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive.
The definition balances present needs with the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; it neither rejects development nor prohibits resource use.

secs.t: Approaches to development → economist

x: The capability approach is associated with Amartya Sen; the basic needs approach with the ILO and Paul Streeten; the income approach with the conventional or classical approach; and the welfare approach with Pigou.
The income approach focuses on national and per capita real income, while the welfare approach gives primacy to welfare; NEW is associated with Samuelson and MEW with Nordhaus-Tobin.
The correct matching is Nurkse–vicious circle, Rosenstein-Rodan–Big Push, Leibenstein–critical minimum effort and Sen–capability approach.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The combination of high growth with inadequate well-being, declining real wages and unemployment reflects the
high growth–low well-being paradox

All four statements are correct for the stated 2025–26 first advance estimates: GSDP ₹17.62 lakh crore, growth 10.75%, AP per capita income ₹2,94,507 against India’s ₹2,19,575, and Visakhapatnam ranking first in district PCI.
Swarna Andhra @2047 targets GSDP of ₹308 lakh crore, per capita income of ₹55 lakh and growth above 15%, with progress tracked through 651 KPIs.
The distinction highlighted is that welfare often refers to immediate redistribution, while development is a broader process involving sustained improvement in economic and social conditions.

rows.title: Distributive justice and inclusive growth - concept, indicators, policy instruments

secs.t: Pillars of India's inclusive growth model (development-economics view)

x: Exam angle: a direct "three pillars" recall question; do not confuse with the 11th Plan's components of inclusive growth (below).
Inclusive growth considers both the pace and pattern of growth, including who receives the benefits, gender balance and regional balance.
The governmental framing is expressed as “Sabka Saath Sabka Vikas aur Sabka Vishwas”.

secs.t: Bhagwati-Sen debate - growth first vs social investment first

x: Why Growth Matters
, published in 2013, is associated with Jagdish Bhagwati and Arvind Panagariya.
An Uncertain Glory
, published in 2013, is associated with Amartya Sen and Jean Dreze.
Development as Freedom is associated with Sen's capability approach, while the Kerala Model illustrates high health and education outcomes at modest income.

secs.t: Inclusive growth as a Five Year Plan theme

x: The
Eleventh Five Year Plan
, covering 2007–12, first made inclusive growth an objective.
All three statements are correct: the target was 9 percent with a rise to 10 percent, the investment-rate target rose from 32 percent to 37 percent, and actual growth was about 8 percent.
The components included agricultural growth, employment and poverty reduction, reduction of regional and other disparities, and equitable growth.

secs.t: Instruments of inclusive growth - which help, which do not

x: Inclusive growth is not expected from a high national-income growth rate alone; rural development, agriculture and farm credit are important supporting instruments.
The identified target segments include
marginal farmers, landless labourers and SC/ST communities
; the focus is not limited to persons in semi-urban areas.
The VB-G RAM G Act replaces MGNREGA from 1 July 2026, provides 125 days of employment and fixes a base wage of ₹300 per day.

secs.t: Distributive justice - constitutional basis

x: Article 38 seeks a social order based on social, economic and political justice and directs the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.
Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

secs.t: Inclusive growth indicators - poverty, jobs, access, regional and gender gaps

x: GDP, industrial output and employment are measures of growth, whereas HDI, poverty rates, literacy, access to basic services and gender equality indicate inclusive development.
The stated estimate places unemployment among tertiary-educated youth at
29 percent
The stated poverty thresholds show substantial declines, while the earnings ratio between the top and bottom deciles was 13:1 in 2023–24.

secs.t: Trickle-down vs direct attack on poverty

x: VB-G RAM G and DAY-NRLM
are identified as examples of direct poverty-attack measures.
The
bottom-up
approach relies on community participation, for which the self-help group movement is an example.
Trickle-down corresponds to the early Plans’ growth-first strategy; direct attack to ‘Garibi Hatao’; welfare to Nordic states; and bottom-up to the SHG movement.

secs.t: Inclusive Development Index (World Economic Forum) - India's position

x: The WEF’s IDI measures development
beyond GDP
by incorporating growth, inclusion and sustainability-related dimensions.
The three pillars are growth and development, inclusion, and intergenerational equity and sustainability.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Centre released
Rs 2,545.50 crore
to Andhra Pradesh under VB-G RAM G in July 2026.
Welfare delivery in Andhra Pradesh is stated to occur through
Direct Benefit Transfer
(DBT).
The World Bank indicates falling poverty, whereas the World Inequality Database indicates rising income inequality.
Welfare expenditure is stated as 17 paise per rupee, while Andhra Pradesh's poverty headcount is 6.06%.

rows.title: Human Development Index - components, methodology, India's rank and trend
sub: Group-II M2-A-8: Human development and inclusive growth - HDI, MPI and India's performance

secs.t: HDI origin - economist, first HDR, publisher

x: The HDI was conceived by
Mahbub ul Haq
with Amartya Sen; Inge Kaul was also part of the team.
The report compares countries on
education, health and per-capita income
as the principal dimensions of human development.
Long and healthy life is measured by life expectancy; knowledge by mean and expected years of schooling; and standard of living by GNI per capita in PPP dollars.

secs.t: Components - what is in and what is not

x: HDI is the
geometric mean of the three normalised dimension indices
: health, knowledge and standard of living.
All three pairs are correct: mean schooling is normalised between 0 and 15 years, expected schooling between 0 and 18 years, and GNI per capita between $100 and $75,000.
HDI uses GNI per capita in PPP dollars to permit fairer cross-country comparisons; the conversion is based on 2011 ICP surveys.

secs.t: India vs neighbours and BRICS (HDR 2025)

x: China, Sri Lanka and Bhutan ranked above India, while Nepal, Myanmar and Pakistan ranked below India.
Bangladesh
and India were both shown at rank 130 in the HDR 2025 comparison.
Sri Lanka and Maldives ranked above India, and Brazil, Russia, China and South Africa all ranked above India among the original BRICS members.

secs.t: HDI categories and India's place

x: An HDI value from 0.550 to 0.699 falls in the
medium human development
category.
The categories are very high at 0.800 and above, high at 0.700–0.799, medium at 0.550–0.699, and low below 0.550.

secs.t: State HDI - AP rank and state reports

x: District-level estimates reveal sharper intra-State gaps that may be concealed by State-level averages.
Andhra Pradesh recorded intensity of 41.12 per cent and an MPI score of 0.025, while India's corresponding figures were 44.39 per cent and 0.066.
West Godavari
had the lowest listed headcount ratio at 2.42 per cent and an MPI of 0.010.
The older estimates for Andhra Pradesh were
9.20 per cent overall, 10.96 per cent rural and 5.81 per cent urban poverty
District HDIs prepared by NITI Aayog and State planning bodies show that within-State disparities can be sharper than disparities between States.

secs.t: Human development concept - capabilities; same GNI, different HDI

x: Malaysia has higher GNI per capita, but Chile has a much higher HDI because of better life expectancy and schooling outcomes.
Chile is cited as having a higher HDI than Malaysia even though Malaysia has the higher income, showing that income alone does not determine human development outcomes.
Martha Nussbaum formulated a list of central capabilities, while Amartya Sen deliberately avoided prescribing a fixed universal list.

secs.t: Methodology - dimension indices, goalposts, geometric mean, GNI PPP

x: The dimension index equals (actual value minus minimum value) divided by the difference between the maximum and minimum values.
The goalposts are 20–85 years for life expectancy, 0–18 for expected schooling, 0–15 for mean schooling and 100–75,000 PPP dollars for GNI per capita.
Purchasing Power Parity dollars allow income to be compared fairly across countries with
different price levels

secs.t: Human Development Report - India's rank and top-ranked country

x: The recorded trend was from 0.514 in 2004 to 0.633 in 2021, with a long-term annual increase of about 1.42 per cent and a revised 2022 value of 0.676.
The reported figures are life expectancy of 72 years, expected years of schooling of 13 years and GNI per capita of $9,046.76 at PPP.

secs.t: Inclusive growth - pillars, Eleventh Plan, instruments

x: MSMEs, DBT and SHGs are identified as instruments that can widen participation in growth.
The Gini coefficient fell from 36.8 in 2004–05 to
The RBI Financial Inclusion Index rose from 53.9 in 2021 to
India was ranked
62nd among 74
emerging economies in the IDI 2018.

secs.t: Related indices - HPI, CPM, IHDI, GDI, GII, PHDI

x: IHDI adjusts potential human development for inequality and the gap from HDI indicates the loss due to inequality.
The GII measures gender inequality through reproductive health, empowerment and labour-market dimensions.
PHDI, introduced in 2020, adjusts HDI for planetary pressures represented by carbon dioxide emissions and material footprint.
GDI was introduced in 1995, CPM in 1996, HPI in 1997 and IHDI in 2010.

secs.t: Human capital formation - meaning, returns

x: Human capital formation includes investment in education, health, skills acquired through on-the-job training, migration and information, all of which enhance people's productive capacity.
Human capital formation raises productivity and earnings, promotes faster growth and helps reduce poverty; it does not cause a
permanent decline in labour productivity
Poverty is reported at 35.1% among those with no formal education and 14.9% among those with post-secondary education, indicating an inverse relationship between education and poverty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements are correct: India's value was 0.732; Goa and Kerala were above 0.86; Assam recorded 0.699 and ranked 24th of 29; and West Bengal recorded 0.719.
The policy discussion indicates that the Government now leans on the Multidimensional Poverty Index rather than relying only on income poverty lines.

rows.title: Related UNDP indices - IHDI, Gender Inequality Index, Gender Development Index, Multidimensional Poverty Index

secs.t: Global MPI - publishers, India's value and headcount, poorest states

x: Exam angle: 0.069 vs 0.690 vs 0.096 style options; the value is small because MPI = headcount x intensity.
The headcount ratio fell from 55.1% in 2005–06 to 16.4% in 2019–21, representing about 234 million people in poverty in the latter period.
The Global MPI 2022 reported that
414 million
people moved out of multidimensional poverty in India between 2005–06 and 2019–21.

secs.t: Human Poverty Index - HDR, meaning, replacement

x: The HPI measured deprivation in
longevity, knowledge and a decent standard of living
The Human Poverty Index indicated
the standard of living
by measuring selected forms of deprivation.
The Gender-related Development Index and Gender Empowerment Measure were both introduced in the HDR 1995 as earlier companion indices.

secs.t: National MPI - NITI Aayog, editions, indicators, poorest and least poor states

x: Exam angle: "Which organisation estimates the National MPI?" - NITI Aayog.
The National MPI retains the three equally weighted dimensions, uses the Alkire–Foster method and expands the indicator count to 12.
The National MPI value based on NFHS-5 for 2019–21 was
; its headcount ratio was 14.96 per cent and intensity was 44.39 per cent.

The Global MPI covers nutrition and child mortality under health; years of schooling and school attendance under education; and cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing and assets under living standards.
The NITI Aayog National MPI uses 12 SDG-aligned indicators and adds
maternal health and bank account
to the Global MPI framework.

All three statements are correct: 24.82 crore people escaped poverty, the ratio declined by 17.89 percentage points from 29.17% to 11.28%, and Uttar Pradesh recorded the largest fall of 5.94 crore people.

secs.t: MPI design - dimensions, indicators, developer, method, year

x: The MPI proposed by Alkire and Santos uses household-survey micro-data to identify multiple deprivations at the individual level.
The MPI was proposed by
Sabina Alkire and Maria Emma Santos
Each of the four education and health indicators carries a weight of
The MPI is not a measure restricted to extreme poverty below one dollar a day.

secs.t: Gender Inequality Index - HDR, dimensions, India

x: The reproductive-health dimension includes the maternal mortality ratio and adolescent birth rate.
The empowerment dimension includes women's share of parliamentary seats and the proportion of adults aged 25 years and above with some secondary education.
The labour-market dimension uses female and male labour-force participation among persons aged
15 years and above

secs.t: Capability Poverty Measure - UNDP indicators

x: The Capability Poverty Measure was introduced by the UNDP in the Human Development Report 1996.
Male labour-force participation
is not a CPM indicator.
Underweight children below five indicate deprivation in
health and nutrition

secs.t: IHDI and Gender Development Index - loss, ratio, groups

x: When inequality exists, the IHDI is lower than the HDI because it discounts achievement for unequal distribution.
A GDI value of 1 represents
gender parity
in the measured dimensions of health, education and earned income.
Countries are placed into
five groups
according to their distance from gender parity.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rural poverty was lowest in
Himachal Pradesh
at 0.4% under the updated assessment.
The two estimates are different because they use different poverty lines and count poverty differently.
GDI/GEM dates to 1995, HPI to 1997, and MPI, GII and IHDI to 2010.
MPI, Gender Inequality Index and Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index are associated with 2010 in the stated sequence.

rows.title: Other global indices - Global Hunger Index, Environmental Performance Index, Ease of Doing Business, Global Innovation Index, World Happiness Report

secs.t: Ease of Doing Business - India's rank, sub-indices, lags, successor

x: The report functioned as a ready reckoner for
foreign investors
by comparing business regulations across economies.
The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (
DPIIT
) is the nodal agency for India's participation in B-READY.
Enforcing contracts
and registering property remained among India’s worst indicators in Doing Business 2020.
Protecting minority investors, getting electricity and construction permits
were identified as India’s strongest indicators in DB 2020.

secs.t: Index → publisher

x: The Global Hunger Index is published by Concern Worldwide of Ireland and Welthungerhilfe of Germany.
WIPO co-publishes the Global Innovation Index with Cornell University and INSEAD; this association dates from 2007.
The Agriculture Orientation Index is published by FAO, not IFPRI.
WIPO was established in 1967, is a UN agency headquartered in Geneva and has 193 members.

secs.t: Index → components/indicators

x: The six variables include GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity and perceptions of corruption.
Ecosystem Vitality
carried the largest weight at 45 percent, compared with 30 percent for Climate Change Mitigation and 25 percent for Environmental Health.
The CPI covers 182 countries, uses 13 data sources and interprets higher scores as cleaner conditions.

secs.t: India's objections to methodology (GHI, EPI)

x: India objected to the preference for absolute emissions, the neglect of the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities, and the use of contested indicators.
The counter-evidence includes India's 23rd position in CCPI 2026, 50 percent non-fossil installed power capacity in 2025 and achievement five years before the 2030 NDC target.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct: India ranked 176th of 177 overall, 175th in Air Quality and 130th in Climate Mitigation in the EPI 2026.
India occupied the
54th
position in StartupBlink's Innovators Business Environment Index 2026.
Perception surveys and absolute-emission metrics may disadvantage populous developing countries, particularly because absolute emissions can be high due to population size.

rows.title: Environmental degradation as a development challenge; green accounting and green GDP

secs.t: Resource depletion → cause; long-term impact scenarios

x: Deep bore tubewells are associated with groundwater depletion, brick production with topsoil loss, and agricultural expansion with habitat loss.
Green urea uses
green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide
and is regarded as a low-carbon alternative.
Urban particulate pollution and coal-based power
are identified as the main reasons for India’s low Environmental Performance Index score.

secs.t: Functions of the environment

x: The environment supplies renewable and non-renewable resources, assimilates wastes, sustains genetic and biological diversity, and provides scenery and amenity.
Absorptive capacity is the ability of the environment to absorb degradation, or the maximum pollutant load an ecosystem can process and neutralise without harm.
An environmental crisis arises when resource extraction exceeds regeneration and waste generation exceeds the environment’s absorptive capacity.

secs.t: Causes of environmental degradation vs conservation practices

x: Wildlife conservation
is a conservation practice, not a human-driven cause of environmental degradation.
Deforestation, chemical-intensive farming and overfishing are human-driven causes.
India faces poverty-induced degradation as well as pollution associated with affluence and rapid industrial growth.

secs.t: Green economy and green GDP

x: A green economy reduces environmental risks and ecological scarcities and seeks development decoupled from resource use and pollution.
Uttarakhand
was the first Indian State to adopt green GDP in the form of Gross Environment Product.
NEW is associated with Paul Samuelson, while MEW is associated with Nordhaus and Tobin.
Green GDP adjusts conventional GDP for environmental consequences, particularly resource depletion and environmental degradation.

secs.t: Growth-environment trade-off vs protection as a necessity

x: The trade-off view argues that environmental rules can slow growth and reflects the ‘grow first, clean up later’ approach associated with Environmental Kuznets Curve logic.
Environmental degradation raises health costs and lowers labour efficiency
; therefore, protection can support long-term prosperity rather than merely impose a short-term cost.
EIA was first used in 1978 for river valley projects; the notification dates are 1994 and 2006, and clearance is compulsory for 39 project categories.

secs.t: Green accounting frameworks → developer; MoSPI EnviStats

x: The
Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
compiles environment accounts based on SEEA and has released ecosystem and natural-asset accounts since 2018.
EnviStats India is an annual MoSPI publication based on the United Nations Statistics Division’s FDES 2013.
EnviStats India covers conditions and quality, resources and use, residuals, extreme events, human settlements and health, and protection and management.

secs.t: Cost of environmental degradation to India (World Bank)

x: The World Bank estimated India's annual cost of environmental degradation at about
of GDP in 2013.
The estimated annual cost was Rs 3.75 lakh crore for 2009.
Environmental degradation raises healthcare expenditure and reduces labour productivity, creating a combined economic cost.

secs.t: Land degradation and desertification - ISRO atlas, AP districts

x: The Atlas estimated 97.85 million hectares, equivalent to 29.77% of India's area, as degraded during 2018–19.
All three statements are correct: the area rose from 94.53 to 97.85 million hectares, the share from 28.8% to 29.77%, and the increase was about 2.2 lakh hectares annually.
Water erosion accounted for 10.98% and vegetation degradation for 8.91%, making them the leading processes mentioned.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India's second land-restoration progress report was presented in the context of
UNCCD COP17
The AP Common Zoning Regulations 2026 provide for
nine
land-use categories.
Forests, hills, water bodies, eco-sensitive areas and Coastal Regulation Zone areas are development-restricted under the regulations.
Conventional GDP does not account for the depletion of natural resources; consequently, recorded growth can coexist with a loss of natural capital.

rows.title: Sustainable development - definition, Brundtland Report, SDGs and India's progress

secs.t: First definition and milestones; Brundtland Report

x: The
World Commission on Environment and Development
, popularly called the Brundtland Commission, is credited with first defining sustainable development in Our Common Future.
The Club of Rome milestone is associated with 1968, Limits to Growth was published in 1972, Our Common Future was published in 1987, and the Rio Earth Summit took place in 1992.

secs.t: SDGs number game

x: Exam angle: 169 targets vs distractors 99, 129, 150.
The SDGs were adopted at the
70th session
of the UN General Assembly as part of the 2030 Agenda.
India’s National Indicator Framework 2026 contains 277 indicators and is associated with the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
The MDGs consisted of 8 goals for the period 2000–2015.

secs.t: Three pillars of sustainability

x: Sustainable development seeks a balance among economic growth, social inclusion and environmental protection rather than maximising one pillar alone.
The socio-environmental overlap combines social concerns with environmental protection.

secs.t: Basic goal of sustainable development

x: The core goal is to meet present needs without reducing the options available to future generations, within the Earth’s carrying capacity.

secs.t: Agenda 2030 principles and roots

x: Agenda 2030 is universal, interconnected, inclusive and participatory, and is guided by the principle of leaving no one behind.
A specific focus of Agenda 2030 is ending all discrimination and violence against
women and girls
Agenda 2030 grew from the Millennium Development Goals and the outcome of the Rio+20 Conference.

secs.t: Related concepts - carrying capacity, Earth Overshoot Day, intergenerational equity

x: The finite carrying capacity of the Earth is a concern reflected in Limits to Growth, Our Common Future and the 1992 UNCED process.
Earth Overshoot Day marks the point when humanity’s demand on nature in a year exceeds what the Earth can regenerate during that year.
The precautionary principle, polluter pays principle and common but differentiated responsibilities were endorsed at Rio 1992.

secs.t: India's SDG progress - SDSN rank, Voluntary National Reviews

x: India was ranked
94th
in the SDSN Sustainable Development Report 2026, its highest-ever position.
In the 2025 SDSN report, India ranked 99th out of 167, scored approximately 67, and entered the top 100 for the first time.
Finland
was the highest-ranked country in the 2025 SDSN Sustainable Development Report, followed by Sweden and Denmark.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs is aligned with
SDG 11
, which concerns sustainable cities and communities.
India continues to trail smaller South Asian neighbours and is off track on 13 of the 17 SDGs.
All three statements are correct: the relaunch occurred on 2 May 2025, Land Pooling Scheme 2.0 commenced, and the UN-Habitat partnership concerns a Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs.
