rows.title: MSMEs - definition, contribution, problems, credit guarantee and support schemes
sub: Group-II M2-A-62: MSMEs - definition, role, problems and support schemes

secs.t: MSME definition - basis of classification, revision history, micro/small/medium thresholds

x: Exam angle: "small enterprise is defined on the basis of" → investment in P&M/equipment AND annual turnover.
The post-2020 classification uses a composite criterion of investment in plant and machinery or equipment together with annual turnover.
The major milestones were the ₹5 lakh ceiling in 1950, the 1991 increase, separate 2006 limits, and the composite criterion notified on 1 June 2020.
Under the 2020 limits, a
small enterprise
could have investment up to ₹10 crore and turnover up to ₹50 crore.
All three pairs correctly state the revised limits from 1 April 2025: ₹2.5/10 crore for micro, ₹25/100 crore for small, and ₹125/500 crore for medium enterprises.
Andhra Pradesh defines mega projects as projects providing 2,000 or more direct jobs.

secs.t: MSMED Act 2006 - year passed, original definitions for manufacturing and services

x: The Bill introduced on 12 May 2005 became the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006.
The original 2006 manufacturing ceiling for a
micro enterprise
was investment up to ₹25 lakh in plant and machinery.
Disputes concerning delayed payments are referred to the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council.

secs.t: SIDBI - year established, role, partnerships for MSME finance

x: CGTMSE was co-founded by the Ministry of MSME and SIDBI in 2000 to provide credit guarantee support for collateral-free lending.
TReDS is an online platform mechanism for discounting MSME invoices and improving their working-capital access.

The Budget 2026-27 measures include settlement of all CPSE purchases from MSMEs on TReDS, CGTMSE guarantees for TReDS discounting, a GeM-TReDS link and treatment of receivables as asset-backed securities.

secs.t: SSI reservation - number of reserved items over time, dereservation committee

x: Reservation began in 1967, peaked at about 873 items in 1984, the Abid Hussain Committee made its recommendations in 1997, and the last 20 items were dereserved in 2015.
Reservation for the small-scale sector began in 1967 with 47 items.
The last 20 items were dereserved in 2015, completing the phasing out of SSI reservation.

secs.t: Role of small and cottage industries - employment, dispersal, concentration of economic power, small-scale policies

x: Small industries are labour-intensive, require little capital and help disperse industrial activity to rural and semi-urban areas.
Small industries disperse ownership of wealth and economic activity, thereby reducing the concentration of economic power.
The IPR 1948 identified difficulties relating to raw materials, finance, marketing and technology.
The Karve Committee proposed avoiding technological unemployment, maximising employment during the Second Plan and promoting decentralised development.

secs.t: Small-scale sector committees - Nayak, Abid Hussain, Karve

x: The Karve Committee was constituted in 1955 in connection with village and small industries in the Second Plan.
Karve relates to village and small industries; Nayak to working-capital credit; Abid Hussain to deregulation and competitiveness; and U.K. Sinha to MSME finance, stressed assets and timely payments.
The correct sequence is Karve (1955), Nayak (1992), Abid Hussain (1997), S.P. Gupta (2001) and U.K. Sinha (2019).

secs.t: Contribution - share in GVA, exports, employment, number of enterprises

x: The 2023–24 LENSD figures are approximately 31 per cent of GDP, 35 per cent of manufacturing output and 45 per cent of exports.
MSMEs act as ancillary units to large industries, reduce regional imbalances and spread ownership of wealth more evenly.
APSES 2024–25 retained the older figures of 8 per cent of GDP and 40 per cent of exports; later estimates supersede them.

secs.t: Credit and payments - CGTMSE, PMMY, ECLGS, TReDS, State Finance Corporations

x: PMMY or MUDRA provides collateral-free loans up to ₹20 lakh through
Shishu, Kishor, Tarun and Tarun Plus
TReDS platforms are RBI-regulated, discount eligible MSME receivables from corporates, government and PSUs, and include RXIL, M1xchange and Invoicemart.
The RBI position stated that no collateral is required for MSE loans up to
₹20 lakh
; banks may go up to ₹25 lakh.

secs.t: AP MSME policy - AP MSME Development Policy, MSME parks, YSR Navodayam

x: The AP MSME and Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 covers 2024–29, was issued through G.O.Ms.No.71 on 26 October 2024, and provides a 25 per cent capital subsidy.
The revamped Andhra Pradesh MSME Policy 2026 adds incentives for
women-led MSMEs
YSR Navodayam was launched in 2019 for one-time restructuring of stressed MSME loans.

secs.t: Entrepreneurship schemes - Stand-Up India, Startup India, Udyam Abhilasha, PMEGP, Udyam

x: A non-individual enterprise qualifies when at least
51 per cent
of its shareholding and control is held by SC/ST persons or women.
PMEGP was formed in 2008 by merging the Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) and the Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP).
Udyam Registration, introduced in 2020, is free, paperless and based on self-declaration; it is linked with GeM, income tax, GST and TReDS.

secs.t: Khadi and village industries - KVIC, PM Vishwakarma, traditional industries

x: The Ministry of MSME was formed in 2007 by merging the Ministry of Small-Scale Industries with the Ministry of
Agro and Rural Industries

PM Vishwakarma provides an identity card, skilling support, a toolkit incentive up to ₹15,000 and collateral-free credit up to ₹3 lakh at 5 per cent; it does not require equity investment in listed companies.

secs.t: Problems - credit gap, delayed payments (SAMADHAAN), technology, marketing

x: The Samadhaan mechanism addresses delayed payments under the MSMED Act’s
45-day payment rule

The identified problems include obsolete technology, weak marketing and exports, compliance burden, skill deficit and costly or inadequate credit; excessive access to cheap credit is not a problem listed here.

secs.t: ECLGS, RAMP, MSE-CDP, Self-Reliant India Fund

x: ECLGS was a COVID-19 credit-guarantee line for MSMEs, while World Bank-supported RAMP focuses on institutions, market access and credit.
MSE-CDP supports cluster common facilities and industrial parks.
The Self-Reliant India Fund provides equity for MSMEs through
daughter funds
Budget 2026–27 announced an SME Growth Fund of
₹10,000 crore
, along with Champion MSMEs.

secs.t: Public procurement policy - mandatory share and sub-targets

x: The mandatory procurement share from MSEs is
25 per cent
; it was raised from 20 per cent in 2018.
The sub-targets are
4 per cent from SC/ST-owned MSEs and 3 per cent from women-owned MSEs
The cited GeM figures are ₹18.4 lakh crore in GMV and participation by more than 11 lakh MSEs.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026 makes TReDS settlement mandatory for CPSEs.
More than 2.56 lakh Samadhaan cases involving ₹55,244 crore were cited, highlighting the delayed-payment problem.
The Ministry of MSME was formed in 2007, PMEGP was formed in 2008, Stand-Up India was launched in 2016 and Udyam Registration was introduced in 2020.

rows.title: Industrial policy - resolutions of 1948, 1956, 1977, 1980 and the New Industrial Policy 1991
sub: Group-II M2-A-56: Industrial policy in India - 1948, 1956 and 1977 resolutions
Group-II M2-A-57: New Industrial Policy 1991 - features, delicensing and its impact

secs.t: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 - schedules, Plan basis, epithet, licensing

x: Exam angle: "Which resolution formed the basis of the Second Plan?" - IPR 1956.
The 1956 Resolution adopted the
socialist pattern of society
as its goal, following the Avadi session of the Indian National Congress in 1955.
Machine tools
were included in Schedule B. Arms and ammunition and railways were associated with Schedule A, while textiles were among centrally regulated industries under the 1948 policy.

secs.t: Industrial Policy Resolution 1948 - categories, economic system, joint sector

x: The 1948 Resolution defined roles for both the public and private sectors and thereby laid the foundation of a
mixed economy
Coal, mineral oils, iron and steel, aircraft,
shipbuilding
and telephone/telegraph apparatus formed the six mixed-sector industries.
Salt, automobiles, heavy chemicals,
fertilizers
, cement, sugar, paper and textiles were among the centrally regulated industries.

secs.t: New Industrial Policy 1991 - licensing, public sector, MRTP, FDI, criticism, licensed industries

x: Licensing was initially abolished except for 18 industries and was later reduced to five industries: alcohol, cigarettes and tobacco, electronic aerospace and defence equipment, industrial explosives, and hazardous chemicals.
Criticisms included jobless growth, regional imbalance, distress of small units from cheap imports, import dependence and environmental damage.
Licensing was retained for selected sensitive industries, including
alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals and industrial explosives
, as well as electronics, aerospace, drugs and pharmaceuticals.

secs.t: Industrial Policy Statement 1977 - emphasis, institutions

x: The 1977 policy emphasised small-scale and tiny units, khadi and handlooms, and employment generation.
DICs were established in every district to provide integrated support to small and cottage industries under one roof.
DICs supported credit, raw materials, machinery and marketing for small and cottage industries; monetary policy was not their function.
The policy used the
MRTP and FERA
frameworks to curb the influence of large industrial houses.

secs.t: Industrial policy institutions - DIPP / DPIIT

x: DPIIT’s mandate includes Startups, FDI policy, industrial corridors and IPR matters relating to patents, trademarks, designs and geographical indications, along with Make in India, PLI, PM GatiShakti NMP and ease of doing business.
The 1991 reforms ended the licence-permit-quota raj by removing industrial licensing, expansion limits, price controls and import-export restrictions.

secs.t: AP industrial policies - IDP 2020-23 and successor, sector policies, thrust areas, validity

x: The targets include ₹30 lakh crore investment, USD 10 billion FDI and five lakh manufacturing jobs;
USD 100 billion FDI
is not specified.
The suite includes Food Processing, Private Parks and EV 4.0 for 2024-29, and Aerospace and Defence and Space 4.0 for 2025-30.
The guidelines for the Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025-30 were issued through G.O. Ms.

secs.t: Industrial Policy Statement 1980 - focus areas

x: The 1980 policy emphasised technological upgradation, modernisation and export orientation, with export orientation receiving strong emphasis for the first time.
Economic federalism meant providing incentives to backward districts, including tax holidays and cheap credit.
The 1980 policy allowed MRTP firms to expand capacity up to 25% without fresh approval, raised SSI investment limits and regularised excess capacity.

secs.t: Industries reserved for public sector - numbers across policies

x: The Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956 reserved 17 industries for the public sector under Schedule A.
The number declined from eight in 1991 to three and ultimately to two after defence was opened to private participation in May 2001.
Defence production
, including arms and ammunition, was opened to the private sector in May 2001.

secs.t: Policy resolution → label or link

x: The
Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956
is described as the Economic Constitution of India and the Bible of State Capitalism.
The Industrial Policy Statement, 1973 is associated with the joint sector concept and the core sector list.
The
Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956
is associated with the beginning of the licence-permit-quota raj.

secs.t: Chronology of regulatory enactments

x: The correct order is Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951; MRTP Act, 1969; FERA, 1973; and Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1985.
The Sick Industrial Companies Act was enacted in 1985, not 1984.

secs.t: Licensing committees → chairman

x: The R. K. Hazari report examined
industrial licensing
and reported that big business houses had cornered licences.
The Industrial Licensing Policy Inquiry Committee was chaired by
Subimal Dutt

secs.t: Reservation for small-scale industries - origin and dereservation

x: Item reservation for small-scale industries began in 1967.
The 1977 policy introduced the definition of tiny units, while the 1980 policy raised investment limits for small-scale industries.

secs.t: Foreign investment and technology agreements - automatic approval, 51% limit

x: The 1991 policy permitted up to 100 per cent FDI through the automatic route in
high-priority industries
, subject to the applicable policy framework.
The present framework follows a negative-list approach, permitting up to 100 per cent FDI through the automatic route in most sectors subject to conditions.
The National Single Window System has been in operation since
August 2022
for facilitating approvals through the relevant ministries and departments.

secs.t: Licensing - industries under compulsory licensing, then and now

x: Automobiles, white goods and leather
were delicensed in 1993.
These successive measures reduced the number of industries under compulsory licensing to six by the 1998–99 Budget stage.
Drugs and pharmaceuticals
were later delicensed.
Electronic goods were delicensed in December 1996/July 1997, and coal and petroleum were delicensed in the 1998–99 Budget.

secs.t: Criticism of the 1991 policy

x: Investment became concentrated in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, making regional imbalance a criticism.
Cheap imports, particularly from China, increased competitive pressure and caused the closure of many small units.
Rising import dependence in electronics, solar panels and APIs, along with environmental degradation, were identified as concerns.
Increase in consumer choice
was an achievement associated with the post-1991 reforms, not a criticism.

secs.t: Public sector policy - disinvestment, BIFR referral of sick PSUs

x: The 1991 policy provided for
20 per cent
disinvestment in selected public sector undertakings.
Chronically sick PSUs were referred to the BIFR, established under SICA, 1985, for possible revival or closure.
SICA was repealed and BIFR was dissolved in 2016; pending cases moved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

secs.t: Impact - growth, M&A, FDI, MSME challenges

x: Gross inward equity FDI during 2022–23 to 2025–26 was stated as
USD 317.80 billion
Gross inward equity FDI was USD 317.80 billion, while repatriation or disinvestment was USD 178.9 billion; consequently, net FDI was falling despite high gross inflows.
India's growth moved from the approximately 3.5 per cent 'Hindu rate' to around 7–8 per cent, and companies such as Tata, Reliance, Infosys and Sun Pharma became global.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The licence raj was criticised for encouraging rent-seeking, creating entry barriers and preventing firms from achieving adequate scale.
The reforms shifted the government’s role from direct regulation towards facilitation, forming the basis for today’s FDI framework and competition law.
Substantial repatriation or disinvestment can offset gross inward inflows, resulting in falling net FDI despite high gross FDI.

rows.title: Industrial sickness - meaning, causes, consequences and remedial measures
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I C-61

secs.t: BIFR and AAIFR - set-up, functions, abolition, successor forum

x: Exam angle: "BIFR deals with?" - revival of sick industries (not stock markets, loan recovery or SSI promotion).
The Tiwari Committee investigated industrial sickness during
and recommended special legislation, leading to the enactment of SICA, 1985.
SICA corresponds to the earlier regime replaced by IBC, BIFR was succeeded by NCLT, AAIFR by NCLAT, and debtor-in-possession was replaced by creditor-in-control.

secs.t: Definition of sick unit - SICA 1985 and RBI definition for MSMEs

x: The original definition included all three conditions: at least seven years of registration, accumulated losses equal to or exceeding net worth, and cash losses in the relevant and preceding years.
The 2016 framework replaced the earlier definition with early identification of incipient stress through SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2 categories and Committees for Stressed MSMEs.

secs.t: National Renewal Fund - purpose, beneficiaries

x: The fund provided VRS compensation, retraining and redeployment for displaced workers and supported industrial restructuring and modernisation.
The Fund financed voluntary retirement schemes, retraining and redeployment for workers displaced by restructuring or closure of industrial units.
The Fund covered organised-sector workers, particularly those employed in public-sector undertakings affected by restructuring or closure.

secs.t: Causes - internal vs external

x: Poor working-capital management is an internal finance cause; aggressive competition is an external demand cause; obsolete technology is an internal production cause; and export-import policy changes are external policy causes.
Delayed payments by
large buyers and government departments
create serious cash-flow problems and are a major trigger of sickness among MSMEs.

secs.t: Consequences - NPAs, unemployment, locked capital

x: Sickness can create NPAs, unemployment and locked capital.
The State took over certain sick private units, especially textile and engineering units, mainly to protect jobs and employment.

secs.t: Rehabilitation measures - RBI revival framework, restructuring schemes

x: The Liberalized Margin Money Scheme, introduced in June 1987, helped reduce sickness in the small-scale sector.
A one-time restructuring of stressed MSME loans without downgrade was permitted in 2019 and extended during 2020-21.
The present framework uses IBC, 2016 and NCLT for company insolvency matters, while MSME Samadhaan addresses delayed payments to MSMEs.

secs.t: Sick industries by sector

x: The sectors especially associated with industrial sickness are textiles, including cotton mills, jute, sugar and engineering.
The public sector absorbed sick private textile and engineering units to protect jobs, but this lowered the returns of public-sector enterprises.

secs.t: Committees on industrial sickness → chairman

x: The Tiwari Committee was associated with SICA, 1985 and BIFR; the Omkar Goswami Committee examined industrial sickness and corporate restructuring; the Kohli Working Group dealt with rehabilitation of sick SSI units; and the Eradi Committee examined insolvency and winding-up, leading to NCLT/NCLAT.
The Tiwari Committee belongs to 1984–85, the Omkar Goswami Committee to 1993, the Kohli Working Group to 1999–2000, and the T.K. Viswanathan-led BLRC to 2015.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The measure required Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) to settle MSME invoices through the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS), addressing delayed payments, a major cause of MSME sickness.
SICA was criticised for protecting defaulting promoters, BIFR references were often prolonged, and BIFR was dissolved on 1 December 2016 as the last SICA-era forum.

rows.title: Industrial licensing, MRTP to Competition Act; disinvestment and PSE policy
sub: Group-II M2-A-59: Disinvestment - rationale, methods, progress and criticism

secs.t: Disinvestment policy - committees, Disinvestment Commission, DIPAM, starting year

x: Strategic sale, Offer for Sale, IPO/FPO and CPSE ETF are disinvestment-related instruments.
Minority sales characterised 1991–98, first strategic sales occurred during 1999–2004, and the period from 2014 onwards accounted for about 70 per cent of cumulative proceeds since 1991.
Arjun Sengupta
’s 1984 work was associated with PSU autonomy and Memoranda of Understanding, not with the later disinvestment recommendations.

secs.t: MRTP Act 1969 - purpose, recommending committee, replacing law

x: The Act was enacted in 1969 and brought into force in 1970; the market-share limit was reduced in 1984 and the asset limit was raised in 1985.
The MRTP Act sought to
control private monopolies and concentration of economic power
and to curb monopolistic, restrictive and unfair trade practices.
The
Dutt Committee
, formally the Industrial Licensing Policy Inquiry Committee, recommended the MRTP legislation.

secs.t: LPG terminology - disinvestment vs privatisation vs liberalisation vs globalisation

x: Liberalisation
refers to removing licences, quotas and controls and changing the State’s role from controller to facilitator.
Globalisation
denotes integration with the world economy and includes measures such as tariff reduction, FDI and the shift from FERA to FEMA.
A strategic sale normally involves a block of shares, usually 50 per cent or more, together with transfer of management control to a strategic partner.

secs.t: Industrial licensing - IDRA 1951, Hazari and Dutt committees, number licensed

x: The IDRA, 1951 provided for licensing of industrial units when they were started or expanded and also provided for Development Councils.
The Hazari Report and Dutt Committee found that the licensing system tended to favour large business houses, contributing to the subsequent MRTP framework.
The five remaining categories were alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, electronic aerospace and defence equipment, and industrial explosives.

secs.t: Disinvestment proceeds - National Investment Fund, Budget targets, strategic sale

x: Since FY24, there has been no separate disinvestment head; it has been merged into Miscellaneous Capital Receipts.
Strategic disinvestment is not limited to sale of minority shares through an exchange offer.
The correct order is Modern Food Industries (2000), BALCO (2001), VSNL (2002) and Air India (2021).
The Bharat Bond ETF raised approximately
₹32,400 crore
HPCL was sold to ONGC in 2017–18 for ₹36,915 crore

secs.t: Chronology of economic regulation Acts - IDRA, MRTP, FERA, FEMA, Competition Act

x: The Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 is associated with
industrial licensing
The Competition Act was enacted in 2002 and commenced on 31 March 2003.
The IBC, 2016 replaced the SICA regime, which had been associated with the functioning of BIFR.
FEMA was enacted in 1999, the Competition Act in 2002 and the IBC in 2016.

secs.t: PSE restructuring - NRF, BIFR, IBC, NCLT, New PSE Policy 2021

x: The National Renewal Fund provided a safety net, including VRS support, for workers affected by industrial restructuring.
Following BIFR's dissolution, cases were transferred to the
NCLT and NCLAT
under the IBC framework.
Atomic energy, space and defence
constitute one of the four strategic-sector groupings under the New PSE Policy, 2021.

secs.t: Competition Act 2002 - committee, CCI powers, agreements, dominance, combinations

x: The CCI was established on 14 October 2003, has a Chairperson and two to six members, functions under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and the Act was amended in 2007, 2009 and 2023.
In 2025, NCLAT upheld the penalty but set aside the five-year data-sharing ban; the Supreme Court appeal remains pending.

secs.t: Asset monetisation - National Monetisation Pipeline vs disinvestment

x: Asset monetisation involves leasing existing public assets to private operators for a fixed period, after which the assets return to the government.
Asset monetisation enables public asset owners to use new financial structures to unlock value from existing assets without permanently transferring ownership.
NLMC monetises surplus land and buildings belonging to Central Public Sector Enterprises, including those that are loss-making.

secs.t: Rationale and use of proceeds - NIF, DIPAM

x: Disinvestment is justified by poor returns from many PSUs, fiscal pressures, efficiency considerations and market listing.
DIPAM, the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management, manages government equity and disinvestment under the Ministry of Finance.

secs.t: Criticism - selling family silver, undervaluation

x: The expression criticises the use of disinvestment proceeds to bridge the fiscal deficit rather than to create or build assets.
The identified concerns include undervaluation, loss of dividend income and national-security risks in sectors such as oil, defence and transport.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The policy emphasis has shifted from selling PSUs towards earning from them, particularly through dividends and asset monetisation, while disinvestment receipts have declined.
Disinvestment receipts have been falling since 2022–23, dividends have been rising, and the Budget does not contain a separate disinvestment heading.
Disinvestment permanently sells equity, monetisation leases assets while retaining government ownership, and a strategic sale transfers a stake together with management control.

rows.title: Make in India, PLI schemes, National Manufacturing Policy; ease of doing business reforms
sub: Group-II M2-A-60: Ease of Doing Business - reforms, India's performance and remaining bottlenecks
Group-II M2-A-63: Make in India, PLI schemes and manufacturing competitiveness

secs.t: Make in India - launch, focus sectors, Make in India 2.0, logo, aims

x: New Processes involve single window and e-Biz; New Infrastructure includes corridors and smart cities; New Sectors include selected FDI areas; and New Mindset views government as a facilitator.
Capital goods, ESDM, leather, renewable energy and shipping are all listed among the champion sectors.
Automobiles, defence and aerospace, pharmaceuticals and medical devices, and chemicals are included in the champion-sector list.
Make in India 2.0 covers 27 sectors, comprising 15 manufacturing sectors under DPIIT and 12 services sectors under the Department of Commerce.
Manufacturing remains around 16.3–17.5 per cent of GVA, below the 25 per cent target, prompting a strategic emphasis on scale, design and global value chains.

secs.t: State EoDB rankings - BRAP, ACI rankings, AP rank by year

x: BRAP was first released in 2015 by DIPP, now DPIIT, with the World Bank Group.
BRAP covers areas such as single-window systems, labour, construction permits, property registration, inspections and contract enforcement.
The seventh edition of BRAP in 2024 contained 435 state-specific reform points.
The BRAP 2024 reform points were organised around
Simplification, Elimination, Digitisation and Decriminalisation
The Business Reform Action Plan was first released for States in 2015 by DIPP in association with the World Bank.

secs.t: Ease of Doing Business reforms - World Bank parameters, reforms credited

x: All five listed items are among the ten parameters: starting a business, getting electricity, registering property, paying taxes and resolving insolvency.
GST, IBC 2016, SPICe+ and online building-plan approvals are correctly matched with the respective areas of improvement.
MCA21 V3 supports starting a business; DILRMP supports property registration; e-Sanchit supports customs filing; and commercial courts support contract enforcement.

secs.t: National Manufacturing Policy 2011 - release, objectives, targets, NIMZs

x: The National Manufacturing Policy aimed to raise manufacturing's share to
25 percent
of GDP within a decade.
Make in India sought to make India a manufacturing, design and innovation hub and set a 25 percent manufacturing-share target for 2022.
The PLI scheme covers 14 sectors, has an outlay of Rs 1.97 lakh crore, and had attracted over Rs 2.0 lakh crore investment and 12.60 lakh jobs by September 2025.
NIMZs are conceived as large integrated industrial townships with zoned land use, clean technology and social infrastructure.
The stated areas of difference between NIMZs and SEZs are size, infrastructure planning, governance, exit policy and fiscal incentives.

secs.t: Recent manufacturing schemes - PLI, PM E-DRIVE, Atmanirbhar Bharat, chronology

x: All four statements are correct: PLI supports sunrise industries, electronics incentives are 4–6 per cent, PLI-Auto has an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, and it requires at least 50 per cent domestic value addition.
PM E-DRIVE succeeded FAME-II, subsumed EMPS-2024, introduced first-ever support for e-trucks and e-ambulances, and supports e-2W/e-3W up to 31 March 2026.
The sequence is 2011 National Manufacturing Policy, September 2014 Make in India, 2020 PLI, December 2021 India Semiconductor Mission, and September 2022 National Logistics Policy.
All four pairings are correct: ISM is ₹76,000 crore, ISM 2.0 is ₹1,27,500 crore, MPMS is ₹62,500 crore, and the raised ECMS outlay is ₹40,000 crore.
The Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme replaces PLI-LSEM and provides a 2.25–5 per cent incentive on eligible sales.
The Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme outlay was raised from ₹22,919 crore to
₹40,000 crore
in Budget 2026-27.

secs.t: Electronics and semiconductors - mobile rank, Semicon plants and locations

x: Mobile phone output rose from ₹18,900 crore in 2014–15 to
₹5.45 lakh crore

All three statements are correct: domestic production accounts for 99.2% of phones used in India, smartphones were the largest export category in 2025, and electronics output increased from ₹1.90 lakh crore to ₹11.32 lakh crore.
The PSMC wafer fab is at Dholera, Tata OSAT at Morigaon, Micron ATMP at Sanand, and Tata Semiconductor Assembly & Test at Jagiroad.
ISM operates under the Digital India Corporation of MeitY and supports fabs, OSAT/ATMP and chip design.

secs.t: Single window systems - e-Biz, National Single Window System

x: e-Biz is a Mission Mode Project under NeGP that enables online registration, filing and payment for businesses.
Invest India was established in 2009 as a not-for-profit joint venture involving DIPP, FICCI, CII, NASSCOM and the States, and serves as the national investment promotion agency.
For a first-time Legal Metrology lapse,
an Improvement Notice
is issued before imposing a penalty.

secs.t: World Bank Doing Business - publisher, indicators, India's rank, discontinuation

x: The Doing Business concept was associated with the
International Finance Corporation
, the private-sector arm of the World Bank Group.
India improved from rank 130 in DB 2017 to rank 100 in DB 2018, a jump of
30 places
The reports were discontinued in 2021 following data irregularities and ethical concerns about World Bank staff influencing rankings.

secs.t: Remaining bottlenecks - legal, land, labour, compliance

x: Contract enforcement and property registration are identified as significant remaining bottlenecks.
The cited figures indicate a rise in formalisation from 60.4 per cent to
75.5 per cent
, accompanied by 77 lakh jobs.
The Reducing Compliance Burden exercise is associated with the
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
(DPIIT).

secs.t: Business Ready (B-READY) successor framework

x: B-READY replaces Doing Business and is intended to provide a more balanced and transparent assessment of the business environment.
The three B-READY pillars are
regulatory framework, public services and operational efficiency

secs.t: Flagship initiatives compared

x: Attracting FDI and global firms to establish manufacturing in India is the strategy most typical of Make in India.
Make in India was launched in September 2014, Digital India in July 2015, Skill India in July 2015, and Startup India on 16 January 2016.
16 January
is observed as National Startup Day, corresponding to the launch of Startup India.

secs.t: SEZs - SEZ Act 2005

x: An SEZ is
a single-window, export-oriented enclave treated as foreign territory for trade and duties
, subject to the applicable legal framework.
Section 10AA provides 100 per cent exemption for the first five years, 50 per cent for the next five years and 50 per cent of ploughed-back profit for another five years.
The proposed DESH framework would drop compulsory positive NFE, permit sales to the Domestic Tariff Area and be WTO-compliant.

secs.t: Electronics - India's rank in mobile phone production

x: India is described as the world's second-largest mobile-phone manufacturer and as being among the top three in volume in the cited reference.
Mobile-phone production value rose from Rs 18,900 crore in 2014-15 to
, at an approximate CAGR of 40 per cent.
Electronics production rose from Rs 1.90 lakh crore to
Rs 11.32 lakh crore
during the stated period, with a CAGR of 19.5 per cent.

secs.t: Atmanirbhar Bharat and logistics

x: The five pillars are Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography and Demand.
The National Logistics Policy was launched in September 2022, PM GatiShakti in October 2021, and the Atmanirbhar Bharat package was announced in May 2020.
Both initiatives address logistics efficiency and costs, which have historically been estimated at 13–14 per cent of GDP.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The stated criticisms include assembly without adequate value addition, concentration of PLI gains in electronics and semiconductors, and failure to meet the 25 per cent of GDP target.
The AP Electronics Manufacturing Policy 4.0 for 2024–29 offers plug-and-play clusters, while semiconductors are identified as one of the state's propelling sectors.
Both statements are true, and attracting investment and expanding manufacturing capacity under the China+1 approach explain how these reforms can support integration into global value chains.

rows.title: Start-up India, Stand-up India, innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem

secs.t: Stand-Up India - target groups, loan range, greenfield, per branch norm

x: The scheme provides loans to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs aged 18 or above for greenfield enterprises.
The scheme operates through scheduled commercial bank branches and supports greenfield enterprises.
Stand-Up India loans may cover up to 85% of project cost, while the borrower contribution is at least 10%.
The scheme had covered about 2.75 lakh loans amounting to ₹62,790 crore by 31 March 2025.

secs.t: Start-up India - definition, DPIIT recognition, NSAC, Yatra, Seed Fund, Fund of Funds

x: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (
DPIIT
) is the nodal agency for Startup India recognition.
Startup India Yatra searches for entrepreneurial talent in
Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
The ₹10,000 crore Fund of Funds is managed by SIDBI and invests through SEBI-registered Alternative Investment Funds; it does not invest directly in start-ups.

secs.t: Entrepreneurship programmes → objective and ministry

x: Udyam Abhilasha is a national entrepreneurship-awareness campaign associated with SIDBI.
All three pairs are correctly matched.

secs.t: Start-up ecosystem institutions - agri-startups, AIM, NIDHI, GII rank

x: The stated support was ₹146.16 crore for 1,943 agri-start-ups during FY 2020–25, with Knowledge Partners such as MANAGE, Hyderabad involved in selection and incubation.
AIM 2.0 continues up to March 2028, with ₹2,750 crore and
2,500 new Atal Tinkering Labs
NIDHI is a DST umbrella programme for converting knowledge-based innovations into start-ups.

secs.t: Start-up financing sources - angel, VC, crowdfunding, credit guarantee

x: Venture capital consists of early-stage equity investment with active guidance for high-growth firms.
Crowdfunding
raises small sums from many people through online platforms.
All four statements are correct: CGSS was introduced in October 2022, uses NCGTC guarantees for collateral-free loans, has a ₹20 crore maximum per borrower and charges a 1% fee for champion sectors.

secs.t: States' Start-up Ranking - categories, AP position

x: States' Startup Ranking Framework
- competitive federalism, assesses states' start-up policies and implementation.
9th
in India Innovation Index 2022.

secs.t: Unicorns - India's global rank, number

x: A
unicorn
is a privately held start-up valued at US$1 billion or more before it is listed.
The government count was approximately 125 active unicorns with a combined value of $389 billion.
India ranked fourth with 61 unicorns, down from 64, and was overtaken by the UK with 70.
The figures differ because the government and Hurun use different methodologies for counting unicorns.

secs.t: AP start-up and innovation policy - AP Innovation Society, Ratan Tata Innovation Hub

x: The programmes of Ratan Tata Innovation Hub are
SPARK, Future Founders, Catalyst and Velocity Labs
The reported APIS figures include 50 incubators, 175 mentors, 564 Entrepreneurship Innovation Startup Cells and 590 ATLs.
The policy provides for a ₹22-crore RTIH-SIDBI Seed Fund, up to ₹20 crore of AIF seed equity, and targets 20,000 start-ups and one lakh jobs in five years.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct: start-ups created more than 20 lakh jobs since 2016, about 48 percent have a woman director, and 53 percent are from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.
Funding raised by Indian tech start-ups increased by
23 percent
High start-up mortality, thin late-stage capital and bank risk aversion are identified concerns.

secs.t: SEZ policy evolution - EXIM Policy, SEZ Policy 2000, SEZ Act 2005, SEZ Rules 2006

x: The SEZ Policy was announced in April 2000 through the
EXIM Policy 2000-01
The SEZ Policy was announced in 2000, the Act was passed in May 2005, assent was given in June 2005, and the Act and Rules came into force on 10 February 2006.
The SEZ framework provides single-window clearance for matters involving both the Central and State Governments.

secs.t: SEZ features - duty-free enclave, developers, minimum area, tax benefits

x: Section 10AA provides 100% exemption for the first five years, 50% for the next five years, and 50% of reinvested profit for five additional years.
The tax holidays were phased out during
under the sunset clause.
The minimum land requirement for a semiconductor or electronic-component SEZ was reduced from
50 hectares to 10 hectares

secs.t: EPZs and free trade zones - first EPZ, Kandla, Falta

x: A free trade zone permits goods to be landed, stored, processed and re-exported without payment of customs duty.
Kandla was India's first Free Trade Zone and was later converted into a
Special Economic Zone
Noida, Chennai, Cochin and Visakhapatnam are listed Export Processing Zones;
Bengaluru
is not included in that list.

secs.t: SEZ performance and criticism - state with most SEZs, exports, Nandigram, Baba Kalyani, DESH

x: All three statements describe reported indicators of the SEZ slowdown: 466 closures across seven SEZs, including 100 in FY 2024–25, and export growth below 4%.
The Development of Enterprise and Services Hubs (DESH) Bill was announced in Budget 2022–23 to
replace the SEZ Act
, but it remains pending.
Nandigram in West Bengal witnessed violent protests in 2007 against land acquisition for a
chemical-hub SEZ

The integration of corridors with Sagarmala is intended to
reduce logistics costs

export subsidies

The PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan was launched on
13 October 2021
The portal, containing more than 1,700 data layers, was developed by BISAG-N of Gandhinagar.

x: The National Infrastructure Pipeline covered the period from
The National Infrastructure Pipeline was originally associated with an investment of approximately
₹111 lakh crore
The approximate shares are energy 24%, roads 18%, urban infrastructure 17% and railways 12%.

NMP 1.0 was valued at ₹6 lakh crore; about ₹5.3 lakh crore, or roughly 89–90%, was monetised, with coal contributing about ₹2 lakh crore.
The shares are highways/MMLPs/ropeways 26%, power 17%, railways 16%, ports 16% and coal 13%.
The NMP is monitored by the
Cabinet Group on Asset Monetisation
, or CGAM, headed by the Cabinet Secretary.

secs.t: Bharatmala and Sagarmala - sector, phases, components, objectives

Multi-Modal Logistics Parks form a component associated with
Bharatmala Pariyojana
Sagarmala's pillars include port modernisation, port connectivity, port-led industrialisation, coastal community development, and coastal shipping and inland water transport.

x: Electrification rose from 50.91% of routes in March 2019 to
of broad-gauge routes by October 2025.
The National Rail Plan 2030 seeks to raise rail's freight share from 28% to 45% and expand Kavach.
The Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor is associated with 1,337 km and the World Bank, while the Western DFC is associated with JICA.

secs.t: Infrastructure financing and PPP - NIIF, NaBFID, IIFCL, InvITs, NHAI, committees

InvITs are regulated under SEBI regulations of 2014 and
pool operating infrastructure assets
for investment and monetisation.
Central capital expenditure rose from ₹5.92 lakh crore in FY22 to ₹11.21 lakh crore in FY26, with ₹12.2 lakh crore provided in Budget 2026-27.

secs.t: National Logistics Policy 2022 - cost target, LEADS, ULIP

PM GatiShakti
by improving logistics efficiency and coordination.
The policy aims to reduce logistics costs to single digits of GDP by 2030.
All three statements are correct: the FY24 estimate was 7.97%, compared with 8.84% in FY23, while older estimates were 13–14%.
LEADS began in 2018 and is modelled on the World Bank's
Logistics Performance Index

secs.t: AP infrastructure - ports, Bhogapuram airport, AP Maritime Board

, associated with BOST in 2004, is described as the largest private port among the listed operational PPP ports.
Bhogapuram airport is being developed by GMR through GVIAL under the PPP-DBFOT model, and its runway is 3,800 metres long.
The APPSC key identified Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati as the three international airports, while Bhogapuram replaced Visakhapatnam's civil airport.

₹1,264 crore
through PM GatiShakti.
Gram panchayats
are reported to be using PM GatiShakti data for preparing plans.
The target for 2030 is
four greenfield ports and eleven fishing harbours
The PPP ports at
Vodarevu and Nizampatnam
are stalled pending a CBI probe.

The National Green Hydrogen Mission targets production of

Bhadla is in Rajasthan, Pavagada in Karnataka, Rewa in Madhya Pradesh and Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park in Andhra Pradesh.

The AP Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy, 2023, was absorbed or folded into the AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024.

Electricity is Entry 38 of the

, enabling both the Union and the States to legislate on the subject.

of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides for adoption of tariff determined through a transparent process of bidding in accordance with guidelines issued by the Central Government.

are identified as measures to boost domestic energy supply.
India’s stated SPR capacity provides about
9.5 days
of import cover, whereas the IEA norm is 90 days.

rows.title: Economic reforms of 1991 - background, stabilisation and structural adjustment measures
sub: Group-II M2-A-11: New Economic Reforms 1991 - background, crisis, stabilisation and structural adjustment
Group-II M2-A-12: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation - measures and impact on the Indian economy

secs.t: Balance of payments crisis 1991 - indicators, trigger, emergency steps

x: Exam angle: the crisis =
high inflation, low forex reserves and a large fiscal deficit
The 1991 crisis was characterised by high inflation, critically low foreign exchange reserves and a large fiscal deficit.

All four factors contributed to the crisis: the Gulf War increased oil prices, Gulf remittances declined, NRIs withdrew deposits and earlier current account deficits had been financed by foreign borrowing.
India pledged
67 tonnes
of gold to the Bank of England and UBS as an emergency measure to raise foreign exchange.

secs.t: LPG pillars - measures, and what is NOT a New Economic Policy feature

x: MRTP asset limits were scrapped, interest rates were deregulated, and private banks such as HDFC and ICICI were allowed.
The Narasimham Committee was associated with banking-sector reforms, including interest-rate deregulation and the entry of private banks such as HDFC and ICICI.
Privatisation involved disinvestment of PSU equity and later attempts to improve efficiency through greater autonomy, including Navratna and Maharatna status.
The initial purpose of disinvestment was to help
bridge the fiscal deficit
; efficiency became an increasingly important objective later.

secs.t: Globalisation - meaning, scope, impact

x: Foreign savings through FDI help fill the savings-investment gap; domestic savings are approximately 30 per cent of GDP.
The IT and outsourcing boom generated services exports and helped cushion India's current account deficit.
More than 1,800 Global Capability Centres were associated with $38.25 billion of services exports in the cited 2026 figure.
Tata, Reliance, Infosys and Sun Pharma were cited as Indian companies that went global.
The pattern of growth was criticised for neglecting agriculture and concentrating growth in capital-intensive sectors, which created too few employment opportunities.

secs.t: Trade and exchange reforms - devaluation, tariffs, LERMS, export-led growth

x: The dual-rate LERMS arrangement was followed by a unified market-determined exchange rate from
March 1993
Import licensing was dismantled, the remaining quantitative restrictions were removed in April 2001, and general customs duty was later reduced to 10 percent.
The reform framework provided an automatic route for investment, allowed NRIs and OCBs up to 100 percent, and permitted FIIs to enter stock markets.

secs.t: Stabilisation vs structural adjustment measures

x: Stabilisation addresses short-term fiscal, inflation and balance-of-payments problems, while structural adjustment seeks longer-term efficiency and growth.
Delicensing, tariff reduction and public-sector disinvestment
are structural measures aimed at improving supply-side efficiency and long-term growth.
SAPs are IMF and World Bank loan packages designed to reduce fiscal imbalances and promote long-term economic adjustment and growth.

secs.t: Persons behind 1991 reforms

x: P. V. Narasimha Rao
took office as Prime Minister on 21 June 1991 and led the government that initiated the major reforms.
M. Narasimham was associated with banking reforms, while Raja Chelliah was associated with tax reforms.
Some liberalisation began under Rajiv Gandhi in the 1980s, but the 1991 reform programme was much more comprehensive.

secs.t: Post-1991 structural changes - direction of change

x: GDP growth was below 1 percent in 1991–92, around 5 percent during 1992–94, and 6.3 percent in 1994–95.
The primary sector's share declined from 38.1 percent in 1980–81 to
34.0 percent
Foreign-exchange reserves rose from about $975 million in 1991 to approximately
$701.4 billion
, providing around 11 months of import cover as stated.

secs.t: IMF-World Bank conditionalities and loans

x: Structural-adjustment loan packages may require currency devaluation, improved tax collection, privatisation and deregulation, along with austerity.
The Eighth Plan, covering 1992–97, began after structural adjustment and macroeconomic stabilisation.

secs.t: Crisis-response measures - taken and not taken

x: The rupee was devalued in two steps on 1 July and 3 July 1991.
Devaluation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper for foreign buyers and was undertaken to help address the balance of payments crisis.
India airlifted and pledged approximately
67 tonnes
of gold.
Demonetisation was not part of the 1991 crisis-response package.

secs.t: Reform architects - PM, FM, labels, committees

x: P.V. Narasimha Rao is widely called the father of Indian economic reforms, while Dr. Manmohan Singh is regarded as the architect or pioneer of liberalisation.
Delicensing brought freedom in pricing and expansion; MRTP reform removed asset and merger controls; financial reform included interest-rate deregulation; trade reform removed EXIM scrips and quotas.

secs.t: Causes of the crisis - immediate vs long-term

x: The Gulf War in August 1990 doubled oil prices and reduced Gulf remittances, creating an immediate external pressure on India.
Two changes of government occurred between December 1989 and June 1991, and the Chandra Shekhar government subsequently fell, adding to uncertainty and instability.
The Gulf War, NRI deposit flight and the collapse of the Soviet Union were immediate external or political-economic triggers.

secs.t: Starting point of liberalisation - 1980s groundwork, what came first

x: The 1980s saw broad-banding of licences, easier capital-goods imports, a higher MRTP limit and relaxation of FERA.
Growth broke the earlier Hindu rate and touched about 5.5 percent, but the expansion was debt-fuelled rather than based entirely on sustainable internal resources.
Devaluation came first in July 1991, followed by industrial delicensing, removal of EXIM scrips and import quotas, and the market-determined exchange rate in 1993.

secs.t: 1991 fiscal policy measures - included and excluded

x: The fiscal package included expenditure control, reduction of grants and subsidies and improved tax collection.
The reform approach associated with the Chelliah Committee favoured
lower peak income-tax and corporate-tax rates
along with a wider tax base.

secs.t: Post-reform direction - global integration, private sector

x: Economic policy shifted from import substitution towards export promotion, supported by lower tariffs and greater openness to foreign investment.
The post-reform approach lowered tariffs, invited foreign direct and portfolio investment, and benefited from IT and services exports as a cushion.
SEBI received statutory status in 1992, while FEMA replaced FERA in 1999.

secs.t: Sectors reshaped by reforms vs largely untouched

x: Telecommunications
was substantially reshaped by private and foreign entry, which contributed to falling prices.
Railways
remained a state monopoly, although modernisation continued to be pursued.
Banking was reshaped through private banks and interest deregulation, whereas agriculture experienced little direct reform.
Private airlines entered civil aviation, and automobiles and consumer electronics were reshaped by reforms.

secs.t: Meaning of L, P and G - which policy each action promotes

x: Liberalisation
means reducing state control over economic activity.
Privatisation
involves enlarging the role of private firms, including through disinvestment and the sale of public-sector enterprises.
Globalisation involves integration with the world economy through multinational-company entry, lower import duties and freer flows of capital and technology.

secs.t: Liberalisation measures - delicensing, MRTP, interest rates, trade

x: Delicensing removed restrictions on industrial expansion and gave firms greater freedom in pricing, except in the limited industries retained under licensing.
The 1991 Industrial Policy abolished MRTP asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and controls on mergers and expansion.
The reform framework envisaged a shift in the RBI’s role from direct regulation towards facilitation of the financial system.
Import licensing was almost abolished and EXIM scrips and quotas were removed.

secs.t: Privatisation measures - dereservation, disinvestment, opening sectors

x: Dereservation
means reducing the industries reserved for the public sector and opening them to private participation.
A private acquisition exceeding 51 per cent transfers ownership and management of the undertaking to the private buyers.
BIFR was established for the revival and rehabilitation of sick industrial units.
Memoranda of Understanding were used to provide greater autonomy and accountability to public sector undertakings.

secs.t: Criticism - jobless growth, crony capitalism, agrarian neglect

x: Crony capitalism is criticised because economic gains become concentrated among large firms with political connections.
The criticism points to lagging public investment in agriculture and the dismantling of food-system supports in parts of the Global South.
Fiscal discipline, tax reform, and trade and FDI liberalisation were among the Washington Consensus rules.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Reforms 1.0 refers to liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation in 1991; Reforms 2.0 refers to digital public infrastructure from 2014 onwards; Reforms 3.0 remains a debate.
The initiatives associated with Reforms 2.0 are digital public infrastructure, UPI, Jan Dhan and direct benefit transfer.
The current account deficit peaked at 4.8 per cent of GDP in
FY13
The appeal sought to conserve foreign exchange by reducing expenditure on fuel, gold and foreign travel.
The Centre established an Economic Stabilisation Fund of
₹57,381 crore
following the stated oil shock.
The post-reform economy is characterised by greater global integration and an expanded role for the private sector.

rows.title: Second-generation reforms and the reform record since 2014; labour codes, IBC, GST as reforms
sub: Group-II M2-A-13: Second-generation reforms and recent structural reforms (GST, IBC, labour codes)

secs.t: Four Labour Codes - laws merged into each

x: Exam angle: Act → Code matching (UPPSC 2021: Contract Labour Act is NOT in the Code on Wages); Industrial Disputes Act year

The Code on Wages includes the Equal Remuneration Act; the Industrial Relations Code includes the Trade Unions Act; the Code on Social Security includes the Employees' Compensation Act; and the OSH Code includes the Factories Act.
The Code on Social Security subsumes laws relating to provident fund, state insurance, maternity benefit, gratuity and employees' compensation.
The OSH and Working Conditions Code brings together the Factories Act, Mines Act, Contract Labour Act, Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act and Building and Other Construction Workers Act.
The Code on Wages applies a
50 per cent rule
to allowances for the purposes of provident fund, gratuity and bonus calculations.

secs.t: First vs second-generation reforms

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2009 key treated "Legal System Reforms" as NOT on the government's list (Oil sector, Public sector, Government/public institutions were), though UPSC notes include it; follow the key if the options recur.

Tariff cuts and industrial delicensing are first-generation reforms; factor-market reforms are second-generation reforms; and fully functional Panchayati Raj Institutions represent third-generation reforms.

secs.t: GST as reform - structural change in indirect tax

x: Input tax credit
prevents tax from being repeatedly levied on tax-inclusive value through the supply chain.
CGST and SGST
are levied on an intrastate supply, whereas IGST applies to interstate supplies and imports.
Article 279A
provides for the GST Council; Article 246A concerns legislative competence and Article 269A concerns IGST.

secs.t: Reforms since 2014 - objective

x: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission and promotes
cooperative and competitive federalism
The Jan Vishwas Bill, 2025 covered
16 Acts and 355 provisions
; 288 provisions were proposed for decriminalisation.
Make in India was introduced in 2014, Atmanirbhar Bharat and PLI in 2020, the Semicon India Programme/ISM in 2021, and PM E-DRIVE in 2024.

secs.t: Factor market reforms - land, labour, capital

x: The framework covers land, labour and capital: land-record digitisation, four Labour Codes, and IBC and capital-market reforms.
DILRMP, ULPIN and NGDRS
are associated with digitising land records.
The stated pillars begin with land, including easier acquisition, and labour, including simpler laws.
The labour-market reform agenda includes
four Labour Codes

secs.t: Ease of Doing Business - India's rank, AP in BRAP

x: India's World Bank Doing Business rank improved from 142 in 2014 to
The World Bank Doing Business report was conceived by the
International Finance Corporation
More than 48,000 compliances were reduced and more than 3,400 provisions were decriminalised.
Andhra Pradesh has ranked first in
every BRAP since 2016

secs.t: Asset monetisation - National Monetisation Pipeline

x: NMP uses brownfield, de-risked assets and mechanisms such as OMTs and InvITs; ownership remains with the government and assets are handed back after the lease period.
The NMP does not involve the sale of government land as its central mechanism; it uses leased brownfield assets while ownership remains with the government.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India improved from 82nd position in 2010 to
57th
position in 2023 on the Market Distortions Performance Index.
The improvement was credited to GST, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), and trade facilitation.
The Codes have been criticised as regressive, the 2026 rules were said not to soften them, and gig workers—numbering 77 lakh in 2020–21—face income volatility.

rows.title: International trade - composition and direction of India's exports and imports; trade deficit
sub: Group-II M2-A-40: Foreign trade - composition and direction of India's exports and imports; trade policy

secs.t: Composition of exports and imports - top items by share

x: Petroleum products
constituted the largest listed export item in 2024-25, with a share of 14.48 percent.
The shares are petroleum products (14.48%), drug formulations and biologicals (5.52%), pearls and precious stones (3.56%), and electric machinery and equipment (3.29%).
Crude petroleum
was the largest listed import item in 2024-25, accounting for 19.84 percent of imports.
Electronics exports rose by 32.46 percent to 38.56 billion US dollars, and smartphones constituted 62.5 percent of electronics exports.
The stagnation was attributed to
petroleum and gems-and-jewellery exports
, while non-petroleum, non-gems-and-jewellery goods performed differently.

secs.t: Direction of trade - destinations, sources, largest partner

x: China
became India’s largest trading partner in FY 2025-26, with bilateral trade of 151.1 billion US dollars, overtaking the United States.
India’s major imports from China include
APIs, solar photovoltaic cells, semiconductor chips and telecom machinery
According to the calendar-year 2025 figures, India-China trade was 155.62 billion US dollars and India’s deficit was 116.12 billion US dollars.
China
became India’s largest trading partner in FY 2025–26, with trade valued at US$151.1 billion, overtaking the United States.

secs.t: Trade deficit - merchandise vs services, causes, record

x: The merchandise trade deficit in FY25 was
$283.5 billion
, representing an increase of 17.6%.
The merchandise trade deficit for FY26 was reported at
$337.3 billion
, with the fourth quarter alone accounting for $83.4 billion.
Services performed well and generated a surplus; therefore, lacklustre services performance was not a cause of the widening trade deficit.
India recorded a trade surplus only in
during the period referred to in the material.
The 1991 New Trade Policy shifted from import substitution and quantitative restrictions to a price-based regime, accompanied by a two-step rupee devaluation in July 1991.

secs.t: Services trade - share, rank, cushion

x: India held a 4.3% share in world commercial services exports, ranked eighth as an exporter, and ranked ninth as an importer with a 3.4% share.
The services surplus, especially from IT and IT-enabled services, together with remittances, offsets a substantial part of the merchandise deficit.
Services accounted for about
of India's total exports, compared with 39% in 2014.

secs.t: Trade theory terms

x: Net terms of trade equals the export price index divided by the import price index, multiplied by 100.
According to Adam Smith's concept, absolute advantage means producing a good at a lower absolute cost than others.
Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage focuses on specialising in the good with the lower opportunity cost.
Rules of origin establish
the national source of a product
and help determine eligibility for free-trade agreement concessions.

secs.t: India's share in world merchandise exports - trend and rank

x: India's share in world merchandise exports rose from 1% in 2005 to
All four statements correctly describe India's merchandise export and import position in 2024.
India's services surplus reached a record
$188.8 billion
in FY25.
India ranked ninth among importers in 2024 and accounted for 2.8% of global imports.

secs.t: Export promotion zones and bodies - EPZs, SEZs, AEZ nodal agency, facilitation centres

x: The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (
APEDA
) is the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones.
EXIM Bank provides lines of credit, buyer's and seller's credit, project-export finance and SME export windows.
APEDA functions under the Department of Commerce, the Agriculture Export Policy 2018 sought to double agricultural exports, and MPEDA handles marine products.

secs.t: Foreign Trade Policy - latest FTP, RoDTEP, Districts as Export Hubs, rupee settlement

x: FTP 2023 came into effect on 1 April 2023, has no fixed end date, is reviewed as needed and targets 2 trillion US dollars in exports by 2030.
The stated pillars include duty-free input schemes, Districts as Export Hubs, logistics and better utilisation of FTAs.
The framework operates through
Special Rupee Vostro Accounts
and is intended to encourage use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade.

secs.t: Exchange rate and trade - devaluation, J-curve, Marshall-Lerner

x: Under the J-curve effect, import bills rise immediately after depreciation, so the trade balance initially worsens; it improves later as quantities adjust.
The Marshall–Lerner condition is satisfied when the sum of the absolute values of export and import demand price elasticities exceeds one.
Both the assertion and reason are true, and the immediate rise in import bills explains the initial worsening described by the J-curve effect.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India ranked third in the Global South for
trade-partner diversity
according to the stated UNCTAD assessment.
The comparison is explained through India's
Ricardian comparative advantage in services
, alongside a structural merchandise trade deficit.
The stated criticism is that FTAs have widened deficits with ASEAN, Japan and Korea and have suffered from weak utilisation.

rows.title: Foreign Trade Policy - objectives, incentives, EOUs; trade facilitation and logistics costs

secs.t: Trade policy instruments and history

x: The 1992 measures provided partial current-account convertibility, with 60% of foreign exchange at the market rate and 40% at the official rate; raw materials and capital goods were also placed under OGL.

EXIM Policy began in 1985-88, the 1991 Trade Policy brought the shift to a price-based regime, partial current-account convertibility followed in 1992, and Foreign Trade Policy replaced EXIM Policy from 2004.

secs.t: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 - features

x: FTP 2023 shifts the emphasis from conventional incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support, while also promoting e-initiatives and merchanting trade.
FTP 2023 includes rupee trade settlement, new Towns of Export Excellence, a one-time amnesty for EPCG and Advance Authorisation export-obligation defaults, and promotion of merchanting trade.
The widened EPCG green-technology list includes battery electric vehicles, vertical farming, wastewater recycling, rainwater harvesting and green hydrogen.

secs.t: Trade promotion and export credit bodies

x: DGFT issues FTP authorisations and runs Districts as Export Hubs and the Export Promotion Mission.
Export Promotion Councils and Commodity Boards promote exports in particular sectors and channel Market Access Initiative support.
EXIM Bank provides lines of credit, buyer’s credit, seller’s credit and support for project exports.
NIRVIK was introduced in 2019 to provide
larger ECGC insurance cover for export credit

secs.t: Export incentive schemes - replaced scheme and objective

x: SEIS was a services-export reward under FTP 2015-20 and is discontinued; EPCG and Advance Authorisation provide the stated import-related facilities.
The Export Promotion Mission is run by DGFT, merges the Interest Equalisation and Market Access Initiative, and focuses on MSMEs and first-time exporters.
RELIEF Scheme 2026 provides support for
war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia
through ECGC under the Export Promotion Mission.

secs.t: Export-import procedure - purpose of documents, rules of origin

x: An
indent
is the importer’s order placed to buy goods.
A shipping bill is the customs document used for clearing goods for export.
A
mate’s receipt
is the acknowledgement by the ship’s mate that goods have been loaded on board.
A bill of lading is the shipping company’s receipt and also functions as a document of title to the goods.

secs.t: EOUs, EHTP, STP and SEZ - distinction and benefits

x: SEZs are duty-free enclaves treated as foreign territory for trade and tariffs, and 100% FDI is allowed through the automatic route for most manufacturing activities.
EOUs, EHTPs and STPs export all their output, may be located anywhere, and receive duty-free inputs suited to their respective activities.
The Budget 2026–27 measures were aimed at using idle SEZ manufacturing capacity affected by global trade conditions.

secs.t: Trade facilitation and logistics - AP rank

x: ICEGATE is the customs e-filing portal of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).
PM Gati Shakti was launched in 2021 and the National Logistics Policy was launched in 2022.
PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy aim to reduce export logistics costs and improve trade facilitation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Government allowed procedural flexibility in
export authorisations
in response to cargo disruption caused by the West Asia conflict.
Export incentives were sought for
aquaculture and tobacco
, along with a request to regulate fish-meal exports.

rows.title: Balance of Payments - structure, current and capital account, convertibility, forex reserves
sub: Group-II M2-A-39: India's Balance of Payments - current and capital accounts, trends and CAD

secs.t: BoP structure - current account vs capital account items

x: Under BPM6, the IMF distinguishes current, capital and financial accounts.
FDI, FPI, ADRs and external commercial borrowings
are capital or financial account transactions.
Merchandise imports
are visible trade and form part of the trade balance.
The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.
A current account deficit generally requires financing through capital and financial inflows, including a capital-account surplus or reserve drawdown, within the overall Balance of Payments identity.
The Balance of Payments identity is current balance plus capital balance plus financial balance plus errors and omissions equal to zero.

secs.t: BoP disequilibrium correction - switching vs reducing, IMF role

x: Increasing government spending on domestic projects
can raise demand and imports and is therefore not ordinarily treated as a corrective measure in this context.
A higher import duty makes imported gold less attractive and helps switch demand towards domestic alternatives or away from imports.
The reported weakness in the Balance of Payments was compared with India’s 2013 ‘Fragile Five’ phase, amid pressure from higher fuel and fertiliser prices.

secs.t: Current account deficit - trend, surplus years, reasons

x: In Q1 2026-27, the CAD was $4.2 billion, equivalent to 0.5 per cent of GDP, compared with 0.4 per cent a year earlier.
The Q1 FY27 figures were a
merchandise gap of $86.1 billion, net services of $51.6 billion and net primary income outgo of $10.5 billion
The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about
two-thirds
of the merchandise deficit.
The FY24 external-sector recovery came from moderation in merchandise exports accompanied by a sharp fall in imports.
Imported oil and gold, low export competitiveness and the savings-investment gap are structural causes.
The scheme drew $127 billion in NRI deposits, contributing to a $27.7 billion capital-account surplus and a $20.8 billion overall BoP surplus.

secs.t: FERA to FEMA

x: FERA 1973 was restrictive and criminal in nature, focusing on control of foreign exchange outflow.
All three statements are correct: replacement was proposed in the 1997-98 Budget, FEMA was enacted in 1999, and it came into force on 1 June 2000.

secs.t: Capital flight and external vulnerability

x: Adequate reserves, low short-term debt and reduced dependence on volatile FPI and debt flows strengthen external resilience.
US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.
Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘
Fragile Five
’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.
Weak net capital was associated with PE/VC IPO exits, FPI sell-offs and US tariffs.

secs.t: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees

x: LERMS, introduced in the 1992-93 Budget, used a dual exchange-rate system comprising
40 per cent official rate and 60 per cent market rate
Full current account convertibility was achieved in August 1994 when India accepted the obligations under Article VIII of the IMF.
The Indian rupee was delinked from sterling in
September 1975

secs.t: Remittances - rank and sources

x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.
The United States is the largest source of remittances to India, accounting for 27.7%, followed by the UAE, the UK and Singapore.
The FY26 workers' remittance figure was $110.47 billion, while Q4 FY26 remittances were $31.07 billion, a 13-year high.
Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.

secs.t: Accounting identity - BoP vs balance of trade, errors and omissions, reserves

x: A CAD may be financed through capital-account inflows or by using reserves.
Balance of Trade equals merchandise exports minus merchandise imports and is a part of the current account.
Autonomous transactions are motivated by their own economic purpose.
A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down.

secs.t: IMF role - BoP support facilities, SDR

x: IMF finance is generally treated as a last resort for correcting balance of payments disequilibrium, particularly during an external crisis.
Stand-By Arrangement and Extended Fund Facility are IMF balance of payments lending windows.
India obtained IMF assistance during the severe balance of payments crisis of 1991.

secs.t: Sustainable CAD threshold (Rangarajan committee)

x: The C. Rangarajan Committee placed a sustainable CAD at approximately
1.6% of GDP
and also recommended a market-determined exchange rate.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct: the H1 FY26 CAD was 0.8% of GDP, lower than the cited high-deficit peers, while the rupee depreciated by about 6.5% against the dollar.
Dependence on remittances and one-time deposit schemes may provide useful financing but does not replace stable FDI or guarantee a self-sustaining capital surplus.

rows.title: Exchange rate systems and rupee movement; currency internationalisation
sub: Group-II M2-A-42: Foreign exchange reserves, exchange rate management and rupee movement

secs.t: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects

x: Exam angle: A-R pair "Devaluation improves the balance of trade (A true) because it raises export prices (R false)".
Depreciation is a market-determined fall in the value of a currency under a
flexible or floating exchange-rate regime
Devaluation makes home-produced goods relatively cheaper for foreigners and imported goods costlier at home, thereby switching expenditure towards domestic production.
Devaluation tends to improve the balance of trade because exports become cheaper abroad and imports become costlier at home.
Depreciation can generate imported inflation, increase the domestic cost of oil when demand is inelastic, and make repayment of foreign-currency external commercial borrowings costlier.
When oil demand is inelastic, depreciation raises the rupee cost of oil without causing a proportionate fall in quantity imported, which can widen the current account deficit.

secs.t: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency

x: Exam angle: "which statement is false" - the swapped definition of a direct quote (foreign units per one domestic unit) is the false one.
REER incorporates relative price levels through the stated formula, while a rising NEER indicates nominal appreciation of the rupee.
REER is regarded as the better indicator of competitiveness because it adjusts the nominal effective exchange rate for inflation differentials.
Hedging involves covering exchange-rate risk, and a forward contract can fix the exchange rate today for a transaction to be settled in the future.
A bilateral nominal rate concerns two currencies, NEER aggregates nominal rates against a trade-weighted basket, and REER further adjusts NEER for inflation differentials.

secs.t: RBI tools to manage rupee volatility and stop a slide

x: The RBI restricts domestic banks’ offshore NDF participation and enforces Net Open Position limits to curb speculative pressure and volatility.
The April 2026 action concerning NDD contracts was intended to curb volatility in the rupee and related foreign-exchange markets.
The RBI bore the full hedging cost on fresh FCNR(B) deposits up to 30 September 2026 as part of the measures to attract foreign currency inflows.
Capital-flow easing included relaxation of the ECB all-in-cost ceiling and the Foreign Portfolio Investor route for Government securities, referred to as FAR for G-secs.
A hawkish stance or higher repo rate can attract carry-trade capital by improving the relative return on rupee assets, thereby supporting the currency.

secs.t: Exchange rate regimes and India's regime history

x: In a managed float, market forces determine the rate, while the central bank may intervene directly through forex transactions or indirectly through interest rates.
The Bretton Woods system of 1944 established
fixed exchange rates centred on the dollar
and was associated with the IMF and World Bank.
The correct sequence is Bretton Woods in 1944, the Smithsonian Agreement in 1971, the two-step devaluation in July 1991 and unification of dual rates on 1 March 1993.

secs.t: Rupee internationalisation - INR settlement, Vostro accounts, rupee symbol, masala bonds

x: The framework facilitates rupee invoicing and settlement, promotes INR in international trade and seeks to reduce dependence on the dollar.
SRVAs are maintained by foreign banks with Indian banks in rupees and enable INR trade settlement.
Russia, the UAE and Tanzania are examples of countries involved in INR settlement through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts.
Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad, with currency risk borne by investors.
FII equity sales exceeding ₹2 lakh crore contributed to the rupee moving past ₹96 per US dollar.

secs.t: Rupee devaluation episodes since independence

x: The episodes occurred in September 1949, June 1966 and July 1991 respectively.
In September 1949, the rupee was devalued by about
30.5 per cent
alongside the pound sterling.
In June 1966, the rupee was devalued by 57.5 per cent, moving from
₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per US dollar

secs.t: Determinants of exchange rate and currency-crisis risk

x: In the long run, the
inflation differential between countries
is a key exchange-rate anchor under Purchasing Power Parity theory.
The Economic Survey 2025–26 reported a
5.4 per cent
depreciation of the rupee in FY26 up to January, attributed to US tariffs and capital outflows.
On 19 May 2026, the rupee crossed ₹96.2 per dollar amid Brent crude near $110 and FPI outflows of more than ₹2 lakh crore.

secs.t: Currency swap arrangements - partners and SAARC framework

x: The RBI instituted the SAARC Currency Swap Framework in 2012 to provide short-term balance of payments liquidity support to member countries.
The SAARC currency swap facility has a three-month tenor and may be rolled over twice.
The India–Japan Bilateral Swap Arrangement is a two-way facility involving the exchange of local currencies against US dollars, renewed from 28 February 2026.

secs.t: Impossible trinity and capital flows

x: The Impossible Trinity states that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy.
Both statements are true, and the increased demand for domestic currency associated with large inflows explains appreciation.
Sudden capital outflows can cause sharp currency declines, as illustrated by India's 1991 balance of payments crisis and the 2013 Taper Tantrum.

secs.t: Forex reserves components - order by share, latest size, global rank

x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 reported reserves of approximately
$701.4 billion
in January 2026, equivalent to around 11 months of import cover and about 94 per cent of external debt.
The all-time high reported before the West Asia conflict was
$728.494 billion
for the week ending 27 February 2026.
Foreign Currency Assets measured in dollar terms include valuation changes in holdings denominated in the euro, pound sterling and Japanese yen.

secs.t: SDR - nature, form, basket, allocation, reserve tranche

x: SDRs exist as
book-keeping or accounting entries
in the IMF’s records; they are not physical currency or metal.
The SDR was agreed in 1967, formally created in 1969 under the IMF’s First Amendment, and was originally valued at 35 SDRs per ounce of gold.
Since 1 October 2016, the SDR basket comprises the US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling.

secs.t: FERA to FEMA and rupee convertibility

x: The restrictive Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 was replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, which came into force on 1 June 2000.
The proposal for the new foreign exchange management framework was made in
the 1997–98 Budget
The Tarapore Committees of 1997 and 2006 prepared roadmaps towards full capital account convertibility; the second committee reported on 31 July 2006.

secs.t: REER and NEER - meaning of a rise, base and weights

x: The NEER index uses
as its base year, represented as 100.
NEER is trade-weighted, and its rise indicates rupee appreciation, which tends to reduce import costs but makes Indian exports less competitive.
REER is obtained by adjusting NEER for relative inflation.
The RBI publishes trade-weighted indices based on
40-currency and 6-currency baskets

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The rupee was reported around
₹95–96 per US dollar
through 2026 amid the West Asia crude shock and foreign portfolio investor selling.
The correct sequence is full current account convertibility in 1994, the First Tarapore Committee in 1997, FEMA coming into force in 2000, and the rupee symbol in 2010.
