rows.title: India and the WTO - agreements, ministerial conferences, public stockholding, fisheries subsidies, appellate body crisis

secs.t: Agreement on Agriculture - subsidy boxes, de minimis, market access

x: Exam angle: "Amber box subsidies refer to" - trade-distorting support.
Amber Box measures include MSP and output-linked input subsidies such as power, fertiliser, seeds and irrigation, and are subject to reduction commitments.
Developing countries are allowed Amber support up to
10 per cent
of the value of agricultural output under the de minimis provision.

secs.t: Ministerial Conferences - venue, year, outcome

x: MC1 was held at Singapore in 1996, MC2 at Geneva in 1998, MC3 at Seattle in 1999 and MC4 at Doha in 2001.
The Hong Kong Ministerial Conference dealt with ending farm export subsidies and duty-free, quota-free access for LDCs.
The Bali Ministerial Conference of 2013 produced the Bali Package, including the Trade Facilitation Agreement and an interim Peace Clause on food stockholding.
MC14 produced no ministerial declaration, the e-commerce moratorium lapsed, and 66 members signed a separate agreement barring duties on digital trade.
The declaration sought reform of IMF and World Bank quotas and voting, along with restoration of the two-tier WTO dispute-settlement system.

secs.t: Uruguay Round and Dunkel Draft

x: The Uruguay Round was the eighth GATT round, launched at Punta del Este in September 1986 and concluded in 1993, with 123 contracting parties.
The Uruguay Round aimed to reduce farm subsidies, open services and cover investment and intellectual property rights.
The Dunkel Draft contained proposals made by Arthur Dunkel, the GATT Director-General and Chair of the Trade Negotiations Committee, for the Uruguay Round agreements.

secs.t: WTO basics - establishment, HQ, DG, India, MFN and national treatment

x: MFN requires non-discrimination among trading partners, so an advantage granted to one partner should generally be extended to other WTO trading partners, subject to permitted exceptions.
National treatment requires imported goods to be treated like domestic goods once they have entered the market, particularly in internal taxation and regulation.
India was ranked 18th in merchandise exports with a 1.8 per cent share according to the cited WTO Global Trade Outlook data.

secs.t: Current WTO issues for India

x: The Bali Peace Clause provides interim protection, while India seeks a permanent solution for its food-security procurement programmes.
India argues that MSP procurement for the National Food Security Act is treated as an Amber Box subsidy using an outdated historical reference price.
The two-year exemption relates to fishing in the exclusive economic zones of developing countries and LDCs; it is not an unlimited high-seas exemption.

secs.t: Other WTO agreements and Indian laws enacted

x: TRIPS concerns minimum IPR standards, TRIMS concerns trade-related investment measures, GATS concerns services, and SPS/TBT concern health and technical standards.
TRIMS concerns investment measures affecting trade, and India's compliance involved phasing out local-content conditions.
AoA concerns agriculture; SPS concerns food, animal and plant health; TBT concerns technical regulations and standards; and GATS concerns services.

secs.t: Rounds and country groups

x: The Doha Round, launched in 2001, is known as the
Development Round
and covers agriculture, NAMA and services.
The Doha Round began in 2001, is concerned with agriculture, non-agricultural market access and services, and remains unfinished.
The G-33 is a group of more than 40 developing countries, including India, focusing on food security, the Special Safeguard Mechanism and special products.

secs.t: WTO disputes involving India

x: DS541 concerned India's export subsidies under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme, SEZ and EOU schemes.
The panel ruled against India in 2019 in DS541, and the appeal went into the void because of the Appellate Body crisis.
The ICT-tariff dispute was brought by
the European Union, Japan and Taiwan
and concerned duties on phones and ICT goods vis-à-vis the ITA.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India fears that plurilateral initiatives such as the IFD and E-Commerce Agreement may fragment the WTO by weakening the consensus-based multilateral approach.

The Fisheries Subsidies Agreement is the WTO's first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective, the moratorium lapsed for the first time since 1998, and India joined the fisheries agreement in July 2026.

rows.title: FDI and FPI policy in India - routes, sectoral caps, trends; FTAs and CEPAs signed by India
sub: Group-II M2-A-41: Foreign Direct Investment - policy, routes, sectoral caps and recent trends

secs.t: Sectoral caps - insurance, defence, telecom, banking, retail, aviation, e-commerce

x: Exam angle: "Budget 2025-26 FDI limit for insurance" - 100%; "multi-brand retail cap" - 51%.
The July 2026 relaxation allowed inventory-based e-commerce FDI where the inventory is used to export domestically manufactured goods.
The FDI policy recognises all four categories: fully automatic sectors, government route sectors up to 100%, sectors with automatic investment up to a cap, and sectors subject to a fixed cap.
Civil aviation MRO and railway infrastructure are 100% automatic sectors, while multi-brand retail and satellites fall under the government route up to 100%.
All four statements correctly state the applicable limits and routes for private banks, public sector banks, and greenfield and brownfield pharmaceutical projects.

secs.t: FDI trend - sources, sectors, states, AP position

x: All three statements are correct for April-February of FY 2025-26: gross FDI was $88.3 billion, growth was 18.1%, and the listed sectors accounted for over two-thirds of equity inflows.
Net FDI was negative for five straight months from
September 2025 to January 2026
, mainly due to repatriation and outward direct investment.
Net FDI is reduced by profit repatriation, outward FDI by Indian firms and PE/VC exits through mechanisms such as IPOs.
Net FDI peaked at
$44.0 billion in 2020-21
, before falling below $1 billion in 2024-25 and recovering to $7.6 billion in 2025-26.
Global FDI fell in 2024, India remained South Asia's largest recipient, and the 2026 report recorded a 6% rise to $1.6 trillion in 2025 with the United States leading as both recipient and source.
All four statements describe the Google AI data-centre project: foundation stone laying on 28 April 2026, Tarluvada location, the participating entities and the proposed ₹1.35 lakh crore investment.

secs.t: FDI routes - automatic vs government, prohibited sectors, 100% sectors

x: The government route requires prior approval of the
concerned Ministry or Department
through the Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal.
Railway operations are prohibited except for permitted activities, but
railway infrastructure
is included among sectors permitting 100% automatic FDI.
Trading in TDRs, manufacture of tobacco cigars or cigarettes, prohibited railway operations, and real-estate business or farmhouses are all included in the prohibited list.
Medical devices, NBFCs, construction and real-estate broking, and single-brand retail are all listed as permitting 100% automatic FDI.
The 100% insurance FDI limit was enabled through an amendment to the
FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019
The private-bank cap is 74%, with 49% under the automatic route, whereas public-sector banks have a 20% Government-route limit.
Single-brand retail allows 100% FDI through the automatic route, while multi-brand retail has a 51% cap through the Government route.

secs.t: FDI vs FPI vs FII - distinction and classification

x: Under the threshold associated with the Arvind Mayaram Committee classification, an equity holding of
10% or more
in a listed company is treated as FDI.
Participatory notes are offshore derivative instruments issued by registered FPIs to overseas investors who are not registered with SEBI.
ADRs and GDRs represent equity raised abroad through depository receipts and are counted as
portfolio investment
in balance of payments data.
FCCBs are debt instruments and are classified under external commercial borrowings, even though they may carry a conversion feature.

secs.t: FPI flows - limits, drivers, trend

x: FPI flows are strongly affected by US interest rates and global risk sentiment, and a flight to safety can cause outflows; domestic fundamentals are not the sole determinant.

All three statements are correct: the FY26 outflow was about ₹2.2 lakh crore, March 2026 recorded a net outflow of $13.6 billion, and the rupee crossed ₹96 per US dollar in May 2026 amid the outflows.
India's inclusion in the JP Morgan Emerging Market bond index, with a target weight of 10%, is expected to draw passive bond inflows.

secs.t: RCEP and ASEAN partners - India's withdrawal

x: India withdrew over concerns about China's market dominance, the rise in its trade deficit with China, and possible adverse effects on agriculture, dairy and small industries.
The India-China trade deficit increased from $53.5 billion in 2018–19 to $99.2 billion in 2024–25, strengthening concerns associated with joining RCEP.

secs.t: Press Note 3 - FDI from land-border countries

x: Press Note 3, issued in April 2020, required Government approval for FDI from land-border countries and sought to prevent opportunistic takeovers during the COVID-19 period.

From 1 May 2026, foreign firms with Chinese or Hong Kong beneficial ownership up to 10% may use the automatic route, but entities registered in China, Hong Kong or another land-border country remain excluded.

secs.t: AP's rank and share in FDI inflows
Policy bodies and regulators - FIPB successor, DPIIT, FEMA, ECB

x: FIPB was abolished in June 2017.
DPIIT is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, handles the nodal role for FDI policy and data, and its FIF Portal has been part of the National Single Window System since August 2022.
The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Approximately $40 billion of the $560 billion equity inflows during 2014–15 to 2025–26 was associated with accounting changes rather than fresh capital.
The debate arises because gross FDI can include accounting changes, whereas the amount of fresh capital may be considerably lower, as reflected in the difference between gross and net figures.

units.title: Financial Institutions, RBI and Monetary Policy, Banking Reforms, NPAs, Financial Markets, SEBI, Indian Tax System, GST, Centre-State Financial Relations, Public Debt and Expenditure, Fiscal Policy and Budget

rows.title: Structure of the Indian financial system - banks, NBFCs, development finance institutions, cooperatives
sub: Group-II M2-A-28: Non-banking financial companies, cooperative banks and microfinance

secs.t: Development finance institutions - year and sector

x: Exam angle: "Establishment of which institution began the era of development financing" - IFCI.
EXIM Bank was established in January 1982, supports foreign-trade finance including lines of credit abroad, and is headquartered in New Delhi.
SIDBI was created under the 1989 Act, began operations on 2 April 1990 and initially functioned as an IDBI subsidiary.
SIDBI is the specialised financial institution for
micro, small and medium enterprises
After LIC acquired majority control in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a private sector bank.
The RBI helped set up IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, Exim Bank and NEDB.
NABARD was established in 1982, NHB in 1988, BFS in 1994 and NHB ownership was transferred to the Centre in 2019.
ICICI provided private-sector industrial credit, IDBI was the apex industrial development bank, Exim Bank financed export-import activity, and SIDBI focused on MSME finance.
The correct order is IFCI (1948), IDBI (1964), Exim Bank (1982) and SIDBI (1990).

secs.t: All-India Financial Institutions - number, RBI-regulated, refinance institutions

x: The five RBI-regulated and supervised AIFIs are
EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID
NABARD, NHB and SIDBI are classified as refinance institutions for regulatory purposes, while EXIM Bank is a term-lending institution.
RBI assumed regulation of HFCs under the Finance Act, 2019, while NHB retained supervision and refinance functions.
RDCL received RBI registration in January 2025, had equity participation from NHB and was created to deepen the residential mortgage-backed securities market.

secs.t: Organised vs unorganised financial system

x: An indigenous banker accepts deposits and lends, while combining banking activities with trade or commission business.
Indigenous bankers accept deposits and lend, while also undertaking trade or commission business; they are not defined as persons who lend only in kind.
Farmers, artisans and small traders traditionally borrow from the unorganised money-market segment, including moneylenders and indigenous bankers.

secs.t: NBFC categories, regulators, restrictions

x: An NBFC is registered under the
Companies Act
, although it is regulated by the Reserve Bank for the activities covered by the applicable regulatory framework.
The RBI rejected Tata Sons’ bid to surrender its NBFC licence and asked it to prepare for listing.
A proposal seeks to replace the parametric scoring model with a simple ₹1 lakh crore asset-size test for identifying Upper Layer NBFCs.
AFC, Loan Company, Investment Company, IFC, NBFC-MFI, CIC, HFC and IDF are listed NBFC categories. ‘
Regional Rural Banking Company
’ is not one of them.
Under Scale-Based Regulation, the minimum net owned fund for a general NBFC-ICC was raised from ₹2 crore to
₹10 crore
, with a glide path up to March 2027.
SEBI
regulates merchant bankers, venture capital entities and stock brokers.
All three statements are correct: regulatory control moved to RBI in 2019, while NHB retained supervisory and refinancing functions; 90 HFCs were registered as of June 2025.
Banks’ MFI portfolio fell 40 per cent year-on-year to
₹65,687 crore
in Q3 FY26.

secs.t: Cooperative credit structure, UCBs, AP data

x: The short-term rural cooperative structure runs from Primary Agricultural Credit Societies at the village level to DCCBs at the district level and StCBs at the state level.
Following the PMC Bank crisis, the 2020 amendment brought management, capital, audit and resolution of UCBs and multi-state cooperative banks under stronger RBI supervision.
The RBI indicated that it would resume licensing UCBs on tap after a pause of more than two decades.
Sahakar Sarathi was proposed as a shared-services entity for
rural cooperative banks
Section 75 of the
AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964
provides the basis for the Tribunal’s appellate jurisdiction under that Act.
Production credit through PACS and DCCBs was reported at
during 2025–26, including ₹4,347.22 crore for kharif.

secs.t: Apex bodies for agricultural and rural credit

x: NABARD
provides refinance to StCBs, RRBs and Land Development Banks and manages the RIDF.
Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank reported first-year business of
The notes record 11 Small Finance Banks and 56,193 rural branches of scheduled commercial banks in July 2025.
After amalgamation, there were 28 RRBs with more than 22,000 branches spread across 700 districts.

secs.t: Insurance and credit-rating institutions

x: LIC was established in 1956, UTI in 1964, GIC in 1972 and CRISIL in 1987.
CRISIL was established in 1987, whereas ICRA was established in 1991.
LIC, UTI and GIC were the
public-sector investment institutions

secs.t: Financial regulators - sector

x: SEBI
regulates securities markets and FPIs; it received statutory status in 1992.
IFSCA is the unified regulator for
International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City
, and began functioning in April 2020.
NHB
plays a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies; NABARD and SIDBI have comparable roles in other sectors.

secs.t: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme and JLGs

x: Commercial banks, RRBs and cooperative banks are implementing banks under the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme.
The group-lending idea is associated with Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.
All four statements describe the NABARD JLG scheme correctly.

secs.t: Microfinance institutions - MFIN, Malegam, AP crisis and AP MFI Ordinance 2010

x: The crisis involved multiple lending, over-indebtedness, coercive recovery and borrower suicides; the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh collapsed rather than rapidly expanding.
In March 2025,
NBFC-MFIs
accounted for the largest share at 39%, followed by banks at 32%, SFBs at 16% and other NBFCs at 12%.
The NCGTC guarantee scheme runs until June 2026 or until guarantees reach
₹20,000 crore
, whichever is applicable.
The March 2022 framework specifies a ₹3 lakh annual household income cap, a 50% repayment limit, collateral-free lending and a 75% asset requirement for NBFC-MFIs.

secs.t: Unregulated non-bank intermediaries

x: Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars
are identified as indigenous bankers who accept deposits and deal in hundis.
Professional and agricultural moneylenders are governed by state money-lending laws.
Shadow banking is bank-like credit intermediation outside full banking regulation; NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds are examples.
Liquid debt mutual funds are a main source of
short-term funding
for NBFCs.

secs.t: NBFC vs bank

x: Banks can accept demand deposits, participate in payment and settlement systems and are covered by DICGC deposit insurance.
Banks accept demand deposits, while NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques on themselves.
Banks must maintain CRR and SLR.
Banks have access to the RBI's LAF repo facility, whereas NBFCs do not.

secs.t: NBFC stress episodes - IL&FS, DHFL

x: Defaults by
Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited
(IL&FS), an infrastructure NBFC, set off a liquidity crisis in September 2018.
DHFL was resolved under the special financial service provider rules made under Section 227 of the IBC, and it was acquired by Piramal in 2021.
In January 2026, the RBI Governor advised NBFCs to monitor
asset quality and underwriting
closely.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In Andhra Pradesh, PACS are being developed as multi-service centres, including godowns at the RSK level under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund, supported by a NABARD loan of ₹736.03 crore.
Regulatory arbitrage describes the use of differences in regulatory treatment to conduct activities through less strictly regulated financial entities, a criticism associated with shadow banking.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India - establishment, organisation and functions
sub: Group-II M2-A-20: Reserve Bank of India - establishment, organisation and functions

secs.t: Central banking functions - and what RBI does not do

x: The MPC is a six-member statutory body under the RBI Act and sets the policy repo rate as part of the monetary policy framework.
Section 22
of the RBI Act confers the sole right to issue banknotes on the RBI, except for the one-rupee note.

The RBI’s government-banking function is based on Section 20 for the Centre and Sections 21 and 21A for States, and includes receipts, payments, public debt management, Ways and Means Advances and overdrafts.
The Public Debt Management Cell was created to ease the potential conflict between public debt management and the conduct of monetary policy.
SEBI regulates the securities market, IRDAI regulates insurance, PFRDA regulates pensions and the RBI regulates payment systems.
The RBI frames and implements monetary policy, and the MPC fixes the repo rate.

secs.t: RBI establishment - Hilton Young Commission, Act, operation, nationalisation

x: The correct sequence is Hilton Young Commission in 1926, RBI Act in 1934, commencement of RBI operations in 1935 and nationalisation in 1949.
Ambedkar gave evidence before the Commission in 1925, and his ideas helped shape the concept and design of the RBI.
The RBI’s headquarters is in Mumbai, it has offices at 31 locations, and it is popularly associated with the nickname ‘Mint Street’.
The 85th Foundation Day was observed on 1 April 2020, and the 90-year milestone, RBI@90, fell on 1 April 2024.

secs.t: Currency printing and minting - locations, note features

x: Exam angle: "Bank Note Press is located at" - Dewas.
The Currency Note Press is at Nashik, the Bank Note Press is at Dewas, and RBI-owned BRBNMPL presses are located at Mysuru and Salboni.
The reverse-side language panel contains
15 scheduled languages
, in addition to Hindi and English displayed on the face of the note.

secs.t: Currency management - issuer, reserve backing, denomination, withdrawal, demonetisation

x: The Governor signs RBI notes, the one-rupee note is signed by the Finance Secretary, and the RBI distributes coins on behalf of the Government of India.
Until 1956, currency issuance was backed under the
proportional reserve system
The proportional reserve system required backing in the proportion of two-fifths gold and three-fifths sterling.
The ₹10,000 note was introduced in 1936, demonetised in 1946, reintroduced in 1954 and demonetised again in 1978.
Under the earlier Proportional Reserve System, two-fifths of the backing had to be in gold or sterling, with gold valued at not less than ₹40 crore.

secs.t: RBI offices and committees

x: The four regional representations are North–New Delhi, South–Chennai, East–Kolkata and West–Mumbai.
The Reserve Bank Staff College is at Chennai, while the College of Agricultural Banking is at Pune.
NIBM, IGIDR and IDRBT are autonomous institutes.
The Tarapore Committees, constituted in 1997 and 2006, examined the roadmap to
capital account convertibility

secs.t: RBI governance - Governor, Central Board, Deputy Governors, Governors, accounting year

x: The Governor and Deputy Governors are appointed by the Government of India; the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet approves the appointments.
The four Deputy Governors comprise two from within the RBI, one commercial banker and one economist who heads monetary policy.
C. D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India and served from 1943 to 1949.
Sir Osborne Smith was the first Governor of the RBI from 1935 to 1937 and signed no Indian note because King Edward VIII had abdicated.
Rohit Jain was appointed in May 2026 for a three-year term, replacing
T. Rabi Sankar

secs.t: Regulatory functions - BR Act 1949, NBFC supervision

x: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 covers licensing, branch opening, management, amalgamation, cash reserve and liquidity requirements, audit and inspection.
RB-IOS 2026 follows the principle of “
One Nation, One Ombudsman
” and covers banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs and payment operators.
Under Section 26A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, unclaimed deposits of ten or more years are transferred to the DEA Fund, but the depositor’s right to claim survives.

secs.t: RBI income and surplus transfer

x: Section 47 of the RBI Act
provides for transferring the net profit remaining after provisions to the Central Government.
The RBI earns interest on loans to Governments and banks, gains from foreign exchange operations and fees.
The RBI recorded a surplus of
₹2.86 lakh crore
for 2025–26, described as its highest-ever surplus.
The framework distinguished realised equity from revaluation balances and provided for a Contingent Risk Buffer.

secs.t: Regulatory and supervisory role - liquidity, branches, mergers, winding up, BFS

x: Banks, SFBs, payments banks, LABs and RRBs may open branches without prior approval provided 25% of new branches are in unbanked rural areas.
The rural branch requirement promotes
financial inclusion
by extending formal banking access to unbanked rural areas.
The Payments Regulatory Board draws its powers from
the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
RB-IOS 2026 covers banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs and non-bank payment operators.

secs.t: RBI autonomy - Section 7 debate, Government's powers

x: Section 7 permits the Central Government to issue directions in the public interest after consultation with
the RBI Governor
The MPC framework and inflation-targeting law introduced in 2016 gave the RBI operational independence on policy rates.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: C.
D. Deshmukh
was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India; Osborne Smith was the first Governor overall.
The RBI absorbed surplus liquidity through
Variable Rate Reverse Repo
operations, abbreviated as VRRR.
Special FCNR(B) inflows contributed to surplus liquidity, prompting the RBI to absorb funds through VRRR operations.
Special FCNR(B) inflows of approximately
$136.38 billion
had been mobilised by 31 August 2026.

rows.title: Money supply - M0 to M4, high-powered money, money multiplier, velocity
sub: Group-II M2-A-19: Functions of money; measures of money supply (M1 to M4) and high-powered money

secs.t: High-powered money (M0 / reserve money) - components

x: Other deposits with RBI include deposits of quasi-government and financial institutions, including primary dealers, foreign central banks and governments, and international agencies such as the IMF.
The money multiplier is defined as M3/M0, showing the relationship between broad money and high-powered money.
A higher CRR, SLR or currency-deposit ratio lowers the money multiplier.

secs.t: Indian currency history - paper currency, decimal coinage, seigniorage, legal tender, plastic money

x: Exam angle: "Seigniorage refers to" - profit earned by the central bank/government by issuing currency.
Bank of Hindostan operated from 1770 to 1832, the General Bank of Bengal and Bihar was established in 1773, and the Controller of Currency transferred note issue to RBI in 1935.
The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, put India on the
gold standard
The
Paper Currency Act, 1861
, gave the Government the monopoly of note issue, replacing the earlier private and presidency-bank pattern of issuance.
Not
every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender
; near money such as time deposits and Treasury bills cannot directly settle ordinary payments.

secs.t: Monetary aggregates - M1 to M4

x: Exam angle: "which is the broadest/most liquid", and matching aggregates with components.
M2 equals M1 plus post office savings bank deposits; M3 equals M1 plus time deposits with the banking system; and M4 includes all post office deposits except NSCs.
The monetary aggregate framework from M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the
Second Working Group on Money Supply

secs.t: Demonetisation episodes and counterfeit currency

x: The 1978 measure was implemented under the
High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act
during the tenure of Morarji Desai.
The 2016 announcement withdrew
notes, effective from midnight.
The announcement was made on 8 November, took effect from midnight, and involved both withdrawal and replacement of specified denominations.

secs.t: Money multiplier - CRR, currency-deposit ratio, policy effects

x: The money multiplier was reported as
on 31 December 2025, with an adjusted figure of 6.0 after accounting for reverse repo and SDF.
A rising money multiplier indicates that the banking system is converting reserve money into a larger volume of deposits and credit, reflecting
better financial intermediation
The RBI creates reserve money through the issue of notes, while commercial banks create deposit money by lending beyond the reserves they are required to hold under CRR and SLR rules.

secs.t: Demand for money - motives and theories

x: Under Keynesian liquidity preference, speculative demand for money varies inversely with the rate of interest.
Baumol-Tobin analysis treats cash holding as involving an opportunity cost, making transaction demand interest-sensitive.
Irving Fisher is associated with the quantity theory, Marshall and Pigou with the Cambridge cash-balance approach, Keynes with liquidity preference, and Friedman with the modern quantity theory.

secs.t: RBI's new monetary aggregates - NM0 to NM3, L1 to L3

x: The new monetary aggregates were proposed by
the RBI Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation
, constituted in 1998.
NM0–NM3 are residency-based aggregates that distinguish short-term from long-term deposits.
L1–L3 add post-office deposits, term money and certificates of deposit of financial institutions, and public deposits of NBFCs.

secs.t: Velocity of money, quantity theory, credit creation

x: Velocity is the average number of times a currency unit changes hands in a given period.
Velocity tends to be higher among low-income spenders and during booms, when money changes hands more frequently.
Fisher's quantity equation is
MV = PT
, where M is money supply, V is velocity, P is the price level and T represents transactions.

secs.t: Currency-in-circulation trend and CBDC (e-Rupee)

x: The value rose from ₹17.74 lakh crore in November 2016 to over ₹42.12 lakh crore in May 2026, an increase of approximately
The wholesale central bank digital currency pilot began in
November 2022
, while the retail pilot began in December 2022.
Offline payments, programmability for DBT and a cross-border pilot with the UAE are identified features or uses.

secs.t: Functions of money - primary, secondary, contingent; what is not a function

x: Medium of exchange is a primary function, store of value is a secondary function and basis of credit is a contingent function.
Store of value,
standard of deferred payments
and transfer of value are secondary functions.
The contingent functions include acting as a basis of credit, distribution of national income and
giving liquidity

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The RBI was absorbing the surplus liquidity through Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) operations.
The reported criticism is that demonetisation's black-money gains remain unproven, while cash use and fake notes continue to persist.
All three developments were reported: the CRR was cut to 3%, the multiplier rose to 6.21, and fake currency continued to be seized ten years after demonetisation.

rows.title: Monetary policy - objectives, instruments (CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF, OMO, LAF), transmission
sub: Group-II M2-A-22: Instruments of monetary policy and control of credit - quantitative and qualitative
Group-II M2-A-23: Monetary policy transmission - problems and effectiveness in India

secs.t: Quantitative instruments - definition and current rate (CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF, bank rate, SDF)

x: Exam angle: order of the corridor - SDF (floor) < repo < MSF = bank rate (ceiling).
MSF permits penal overnight borrowing from the RBI by dipping into the SLR portfolio, up to 2% of NDTL under the current arrangement.
The current MSF rate is repo plus 25 basis points, and banks may dip into SLR holdings up to 2% of NDTL.
The bank rate is associated with rediscounting bills and longer-term lending and is aligned with the MSF; the repo rate is the policy rate for overnight collateralised lending.
The fixed-rate reverse repo absorbs funds against Government securities and is now used at the RBI's discretion, while the SDF absorbs funds without collateral.
CRR is maintained in cash with RBI, SLR is maintained by banks in liquid assets, and CRR earns no interest.
The LAF is the principal short-term liquidity-management framework and includes repo along with reverse repo or SDF windows.

secs.t: CRR, SLR, repo changes - effect on money supply, credit, demand, inflation

x: A contractionary policy raises CRR, SLR and policy rates and sells Government securities through OMO, thereby reducing liquidity and demand.
A CRR or SLR cut releases funds for lending and raises the money multiplier, subject to the banking system's willingness and ability to lend.
Supply-driven food and fuel inflation may require
buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms
, whereas CRR, SLR and policy rates primarily influence aggregate demand.

secs.t: Liquidity management - LAF, SDF, fine-tuning operations, I-CRR, OMO, VRRR, sterilisation

x: LAF is the primary framework through which the RBI injects liquidity through repo and absorbs liquidity through reverse repo and SDF operations on a day-to-day basis.
VRR injects liquidity, while VRRR absorbs surplus liquidity for longer maturities than the overnight SDF.
Fine-tuning operations, generally involving short-term VRR or VRRR auctions, are conducted to align liquidity conditions with the prevailing monetary policy stance.
The temporary I-CRR announced on 10 August 2023 was
10 per cent
and was intended to absorb excess liquidity from the banking system.
Under the MSS, introduced in April 2004, the RBI issues Treasury Bills and securities to absorb rupees created by foreign-exchange purchases.
The SDF was proposed in 2015, enabled in connection with Budget 2018-19, LTROs were introduced in 2020, and the SDF began in April 2022.

secs.t: Quantitative vs qualitative tools - classification, most powerful tool

x: Margin requirements and moral suasion are qualitative or selective tools.
Margin requirement
is a qualitative tool because it influences the direction and availability of credit against particular securities.
Variable reserve ratio
, including CRR and SLR, is a quantitative or general credit-control instrument.
The MPC sets the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target, while liquidity operations help keep money-market rates close to that rate.

secs.t: SLR - eligible forms of holding, statutory floor and ceiling

x: SLR may be maintained by banks themselves in cash, gold, unencumbered government securities including Treasury Bills and State Development Loans, and other approved securities.
The
Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2007
removed the earlier 25 per cent statutory floor for SLR.
The SLR stood at about
38.5 per cent
of NDTL in 1991-92 and was subsequently reduced gradually.
CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act and SLR by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

secs.t: Evolution of monetary policy since 1991 - phases, challenges, monetary vs fiscal tools

x: Post-1991 reforms progressively deregulated interest rates, reducing direct administrative determination and allowing greater market and bank influence.
The system of automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997 and was replaced by
Ways and Means Advances
Open capital-account flows affect both liquidity and the rupee, and the RBI can sterilise their effects through MSS, OMO and VRRR.
Oil prices, global rate cycles and wars are external shocks that can affect inflation, capital flows and exchange rates.
Governor
Shaktikanta Das
traced these phases in “Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy” on 24 January 2020 at St. Stephen's College.
The framework was considered opaque because markets could not predict the RBI's actions when growth, inflation, exchange-rate and credit indicators conflicted.

secs.t: Which rates RBI fixes vs market- or bank-determined (PLR, MCLR, EBLR, call rate)

x: MCLR incorporates marginal cost of funds, the cost of CRR/SLR, operating cost and a tenor premium.
From 1 October 2019, such loans had to be linked to an external benchmark, including the repo rate, the three- or six-month Treasury-bill yield, or an FBIL-published rate.
EBLR links specified new floating-rate personal, retail and MSME loans to an external benchmark, improving transparency and policy transmission.
CRR and SLR are RBI-set requirements, MCLR is computed internally by each bank, and the call money rate is market-determined.
The proposed directions retain external-benchmark linkage for floating-rate personal and MSME loans and provide for interest on the
daily reducing balance

secs.t: Monetary transmission - MCLR, EBLR, lags, stance terms

x: EBLR links lending rates directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, allowing loans to reprice more quickly than Base Rate or MCLR loans.
MCLR incorporates marginal deposit cost, CRR/SLR carry, operating cost and tenor premium.
Hawkish policy prioritises inflation control, dovish policy is biased towards easing because of growth concerns, and calibrated tightening involves measured rather than automatic hikes.

secs.t: Policy rates to track - latest and past levels

x: The August 2026 levels were repo 5.25 per cent, SDF 5.00 per cent, MSF 5.50 per cent and CRR 3 per cent.
The CRR declined by 1 percentage point, which is equal to
100 basis points
The SLR was recorded as 18 per cent in September 2023, whereas it had been 38.5 per cent in 1991–92.

secs.t: Most powerful / widely used tool debate

x: Under FIT, the repo rate functions as the single operating policy rate and is the most closely watched signal of monetary policy.

secs.t: Sterilisation and instrument classification

x: When foreign-exchange inflows increase rupee liquidity, the RBI may sell government securities or conduct liquidity-absorption operations to offset the impact.
The RBI may sell government securities through OMO or MSS and conduct VRRR operations to absorb excess liquidity.
The stated FCNR(B) inflows amounted to
$127.23 billion
and created a situation requiring liquidity sterilisation.

secs.t: Bond market and yield curve - what moves G-sec yields

x: Indian G-sec yields are influenced by all three factors: US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions, and domestic inflation and short-term interest rates.
The OMO purchases of ₹1 lakh crore were intended to
stabilise bond yields
and support orderly financial-market conditions.
A narrower spread between Indian sovereign yields and US bond yields reduces the relative cost of borrowing for India.

secs.t: Transmission channels - interest rate, credit, exchange rate, asset price, expectations

x: All five are recognised transmission channels.
Through the interest-rate channel, lower borrowing costs can raise consumption and investment expenditure.
The transmission mechanism proceeds from the repo rate to money-market rates, then to aggregate demand and ultimately to inflation.
A credible target anchors inflation expectations; it does not necessarily remove all uncertainty.

secs.t: Transmission lags - policy rate to deposit and lending rates

x: The difference is 9.26 minus 8.50, equal to
0.76 percentage point
MCLR-linked loans reset at periodic intervals, creating a lag.
The FY26 data cited a 64-basis-point fall in WALR on fresh loans, described as robust pass-through.

secs.t: Obstacles to transmission

x: All four conditions can obstruct transmission by keeping funding costs or market yields high, limiting repricing, or placing credit activity outside the formal monetary-policy channel.
Gross non-performing assets were reported at a multi-decadal low of
2.2 per cent
in September 2025.
Government borrowing remains a factor that can keep yields high; its permanent elimination is not an identified obstacle or feature of the system.

secs.t: Liquidity conditions and transmission - surplus vs deficit

x: Tighter liquidity in December 2025 led the RBI to inject ₹1 lakh crore through OMO purchases along with a $5 billion swap.
Maintaining sufficient liquidity was intended to support and improve transmission of monetary policy to market and lending rates.
The RBI began absorbing the large surplus through Variable Rate Reverse Repo, or VRRR, operations.

secs.t: Internal study groups on MCLR and external benchmarking

x: The RBI’s Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system was chaired by
Janak Raj
The study group found weak MCLR transmission, recommended external benchmarking, and its recommendations led to the EBLR mandate effective from 1 October 2019.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Weak pass-through to deposit rates, the movement of large firms towards non-bank credit, and the RBI’s limited influence over food inflation are all identified concerns.
The specified policy changes included a 100 basis-point repo cut to 5.25 per cent, a 100 basis-point CRR cut to 3 per cent, and the two stated rounds of OMO purchases.
The repo rate does not directly control food and fuel supply; its inability to resolve such supply shocks is a limitation, not a cause of transmission weakness.

rows.title: Monetary Policy Committee and the flexible inflation targeting framework
sub: Group-II M2-A-21: Monetary policy - objectives, framework, MPC and inflation targeting

secs.t: Monetary policy framework committees - chairperson + year (Urjit Patel, Chakravarty, Vaghul, Tarapore)

x: Monetary targeting prevailed during 1985–1998, followed by the multiple-indicator approach during 1998–2014, the glide path during 2014–2016, and flexible inflation targeting from 2016 onwards.
The approach was considered opaque because markets could not easily predict the RBI’s response when inflation, growth, exchange rate and credit indicators pointed in different directions.
Post-1991 monetary policy faced challenges including
exchange-rate volatility
, an open capital account, external shocks and fiscal dominance.

secs.t: MPC - statutory basis, who fixes the repo rate, mandate

x: The 2016 amendment inserted
Sections 45Z to 45ZO
into the RBI Act, 1934, providing the statutory framework for the MPC and inflation-targeting provisions.
The first meeting of the MPC was held in
October 2016
, after the statutory framework was introduced through the 2016 amendment.
Price stability is the primary mandate of the MPC, while growth is also kept in mind.

secs.t: Inflation target - CPI target, tolerance band, review period, who notifies it

x: Exam angle: "In which year was the RBI Act amended for FIT?" The answer is
The flexible inflation-targeting framework uses a 4 per cent CPI-Combined target with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2 percentage points, namely 2 to 6 per cent.
A breach of the tolerance band for
three consecutive quarters
constitutes failure to meet the inflation target for the relevant reporting requirement.

secs.t: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement - terms, division of responsibility

x: The 2015 Monetary Policy Framework Agreement formally adopted
flexible inflation targeting
in India.
All three statements correctly describe the division of responsibility: the Government sets the target, the RBI operates monetary policy to maintain it, and the RBI must explain prescribed failures.
Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the division of responsibility under the Agreement directly explains the arrangement described in the Assertion.

secs.t: MPC composition - members, appointment, casting vote, meetings, quorum

x: The statutory minimum is four meetings a year, while in practice the MPC meets bi-monthly, or six times a year.
The MPC fixes the policy repo rate required to achieve the notified inflation target, and its decisions bind the RBI.
The August 2026 policy outlook referred to a possible hike, average headline inflation of 3.93 per cent, projected core inflation of 4.3 per cent, and Governor Sanjay Malhotra.

secs.t: Failure to meet the target - consecutive quarters rule

x: Failure is defined as average CPI inflation remaining
above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive quarters
The RBI must report the reasons for the failure, the remedial actions proposed and the period within which inflation is expected to return to the target.
The failure procedure was first invoked in 2022 after CPI inflation stayed above 6 per cent beginning in
January 2022

secs.t: MPC decision record - voting pattern and stance changes

x: The rate increases during this period represented a
tightening
stance aimed at containing inflationary pressures.
In April 2025, the MPC reduced the repo rate by 25 basis points to 6 per cent and changed the stance from neutral towards accommodative.
June 2025 saw the repo rate reach 5.50 per cent and a 100-basis-point CRR cut, while December 2025 brought the repo rate to 5.25 per cent with a neutral stance.

secs.t: Objectives of monetary policy - price stability, growth, financial stability; non-objectives

x: Price stability is the primary objective, with growth kept in mind.
Maximising Government revenue
is not an objective of monetary policy.

secs.t: Global monetary tightening - spillovers to India

x: Global monetary tightening can encourage capital outflows from India, put pressure on the rupee and raise imported inflation through exchange-rate and import-cost channels.
In June 2026, the MPC retained the repo rate at 5.25 per cent but reduced its FY27 growth forecast despite global tightening concerns.
The inflation forecast assumed crude oil at
95 dollars per barrel
, partly reflecting risks arising from the West Asia conflict.

secs.t: Policy stances - accommodative, neutral, withdrawal of accommodation

x: An accommodative stance indicates readiness to reduce rates or inject liquidity to support economic growth.
Under a neutral stance, the central bank retains the flexibility to raise or reduce rates according to economic and inflation data.
Withdrawal of accommodation denotes a tightening bias, generally involving the removal of excess liquidity from the financial system.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The flexible inflation targeting framework retains a headline inflation target of 4%, with an allowable tolerance band of ±2%, up to March 2031.
The cumulative reduction in the repo rate since February 2025 was
125 basis points
, culminating in the rate of 5.25% after the December 2025 cut.
Food and supply shocks are outside the MPC's direct control; this is one reason for the criticism of headline targeting.

rows.title: Banking in India - nationalisation, structure, priority sector, small finance and payments banks
sub: Group-II M2-A-24: Indian banking - structure, nationalisation and phases of development

secs.t: Bank founders, headquarters and firsts (Andhra Bank, PNB, first ATM, first SFB, SBI OBU)

x: The Bank of Calcutta was established in 1806, followed by its renaming as the Bank of Bengal, the Bank of Bombay in 1840 and the Bank of Madras in 1843.
Punjab National Bank was established in 1894 and is described as the
second bank established by Indians
Andhra Bank was founded by Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya on 20 November 1923 at Machilipatnam.
The head office of Andhra Bank was known as
Pattabhi Bhavan
Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya founded Andhra Insurance Company, Bharat Lakshmi Bank and the Krishna District Co-operative Bank.
HSBC
introduced the first ATM in India in Mumbai in 1987.
Punjab National Bank
is described as the first bank with wholly Indian capital and management.

secs.t: Banking operations and customer rules - para-banking, cheque validity, ATM penalty, assets vs liabilities

x: Para-banking refers to services beyond the traditional acceptance of deposits and provision of loans, including credit cards, insurance, factoring and mutual fund distribution.
From
1 October 2021
, a penalty of ₹10,000 per ATM applies when an ATM remains out of cash for more than 10 hours in a month.
Customer deposits are liabilities because the bank owes these amounts to depositors.
Borrowings
are liabilities of a commercial bank.
MSE loans up to ₹20 lakh and all PMEGP units must be provided without collateral.

secs.t: Differentiated banks - capital, activities, purpose, universal-bank transition (SFBs, payments banks, Nachiket Mor)

x: Small Finance Banks can lend and must allocate 75% of ANBC to PSL, while Payments Banks accept only demand deposits and cannot lend.
Payments Banks are required to invest 75% of demand deposits in SLR government securities or Treasury Bills with maturity up to one year.
The minimum capital specified for Small Finance Banks is
₹100 crore
, while Payments Banks require ₹100 crore of paid-up voting equity capital.
The Nachiket Mor Committee was constituted in 2013, and both categories arose from niche licences; commercial banks are now licensed on tap.

secs.t: Bank nationalisation - rounds, year, number, chronology

x: The correct sequence is RBI nationalisation in 1949, SBI formation in 1955, nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969 and nationalisation of six banks in 1980.
The second round of nationalisation on 15 April 1980 covered six banks with deposits exceeding
₹200 crore
Nationalisation sought to reduce the control of industrial houses and remedy the neglect of agriculture and small units; it did not aim to preserve exclusive control by them.
Bank nationalisation was associated with expansion of branches and increased lending to priority sectors, including agriculture and small units.
Indira Gandhi set out the intent behind bank nationalisation in a note titled “
Stray Thoughts on Bank Nationalisation

secs.t: State-wise banking data - deposits, credit, CD ratio, AP position

x: Bank credit in Andhra Pradesh stood at
in December 2025; the December 2024 figure was ₹8,61,580 crore.
The ratio declined from 162% to 157.40%, but remained substantially above the RBI norm of 60%.
All four figures are correct: 1.81 lakh branches, 17.36 lakh business correspondents, 99.92% village coverage within 5 km and 58.77 crore PMJDY accounts.

secs.t: RRBs - origin committee, first RRB, sponsor bank, AP RRBs

x: RRBs are regulated by RBI, supervised by NABARD and were allowed commercial interest rates from the late 1990s.
Regional Rural Banks were initially created through an ordinance and were subsequently governed by the
Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976
Fifteen RRBs were amalgamated with effect from 1 May 2025 under the One State-One RRB initiative, leaving 28 RRBs thereafter.
The four merged RRBs were Andhra Pragathi, AP Grameena Vikas, Chaitanya Godavari and Saptagiri.
Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank reported FY26 business of ₹1,36,337 crore and net profit of ₹1,836 crore.

secs.t: Lead Bank Scheme - Service Area Approach, SLBC, AP convener bank

x: The
State Level
Bankers’ Committee is a State-level forum, while district-level forums are run by the Lead District Manager.
Union Bank of India
acts as the Lead Bank and the convener of the State Level Bankers’ Committee in Andhra Pradesh.
The 236th SLBC meeting in Andhra Pradesh was held on
16 September 2026

secs.t: Banking structure - scheduled vs non-scheduled, commercial, RRBs, co-operative, SBI group, foreign bank entry

x: Scheduled banks may borrow from the RBI at the bank rate, repo rate or through the Marginal Standing Facility, subject to applicable conditions.
The associate banks of SBI and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI with effect from
1 April 2017
NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques, and their deposits are not covered by DICGC insurance.
The reported figures were 1.81 lakh bank branches, 17.36 lakh business correspondents and 1.65 lakh India Post Payments Bank centres.

secs.t: Banks → founder, headquarters, year

x: Allahabad Bank dates from 1865 and merged into Indian Bank, while Canara Bank was founded by Ammembal Subba Rao Pai and took over Syndicate Bank.
The United Forum of Bank Unions held a strike on 12 September 2026 seeking a five-day week in public sector banks.
The banking-sector significance highlighted is the 4R strategy for public sector banks and GNPA of 2.2% in September 2025, a multi-decadal low.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Current relevance:
the United Forum of Bank Unions struck on 12 Sep 2026 for a 5-day week, hitting public sector banks.
AP angle:
AP's CD ratio (157%) is among the highest.
Current relevance:
RBI is resuming on-tap UCB licences (Aug 2026).
PMJDY has
58.77 crore
accounts.
A Mega Credit Outreach Program in AP disbursed
₹3,216 crore
with CM N. Chandrababu Naidu and FM Sitharaman.
GNPA at
(Sep 2025, ES), a multi-decadal low.

rows.title: Banking sector reforms - Narasimham Committee I and II, Basel norms, bank mergers, privatisation debate
sub: Group-II M2-A-25: Banking sector reforms - Narasimham Committees, Basel norms, consolidation and privatisation debate

secs.t: Basel Accords I, II, III - pillars, capital ratios, leverage ratio, CCB, LCR, NSFR, RBI vs BCBS

x: Exam angle: match each ratio to its purpose (LCR = 30 days, NSFR = 1 year, CCyB = credit boom); RBI vs BCBS minimums.
Basel II rests on three pillars:
minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline
Basel I was issued in 1988, India introduced CRAR in 1992, Basel II followed in 2004, and Basel III emerged after the 2007–09 financial crisis.
Basel III was formulated after
the global financial crisis of 2007–09
to strengthen bank capital, liquidity and resilience.
The five fixed risk-weight buckets are associated with Basel I. Basel III introduced stronger CET1 requirements, buffers, leverage and liquidity standards.
The leverage ratio came with
Basel III
as a non-risk-weighted backstop to prevent balance sheets from expanding on a thin capital base.
The
Liquidity Coverage Ratio
(LCR) requires a stock of high-quality liquid assets sufficient to survive a 30-day stress period.
NSFR promotes
stable funding over a one-year horizon
, whereas LCR addresses short-term liquidity over 30 days.
In October 2025, the RBI proposed lower Basel III risk weights for
MSMEs and real estate
The capital conservation buffer is 2.5 per cent over the minimum; the leverage ratio caps exposure against Tier 1 capital; LTV caps relate loans to collateral; risk weights can cool risky lending.

secs.t: Banking and financial sector reform committees - official name + year + chair

x: The
Narasimham-I Committee
of 1991 examined the banking and financial system, including capital adequacy, prudential norms and lower SLR and CRR.
The Committee on Financial Sector Assessment, functioning during 2006–09, conducted a joint Government of India–RBI self-assessment of financial-sector stability and standards.
The
Nachiket Mor Committee
on differentiated banking and financial inclusion laid the groundwork for universal bank accounts and PMJDY.
Goiporia dealt with customer service, Malhotra with insurance reform, C. Rangarajan with financial inclusion, and P.J. Nayak with bank-board governance.
The High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat was announced in
Budget 2026–27
to review the banking sector as a whole.
The Second ARC is associated with ethics, public services and e-governance; Ashok Dalwai with doubling farmers’ income; Shanta Kumar with FCI/PDS reform; and Nachiket Mor with financial inclusion.

The Bimal Jalan Committee dealt with the Economic Capital Framework and surplus transfer, the Nachiket Mor Committee with differentiated banks, and the Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee with cyber security.

secs.t: Bank mergers - merged banks + anchor bank, fate of Andhra Bank, expected gains

x: SBI’s associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were amalgamated with SBI with effect from
1 April 2017
The mergers took effect in the order: SBI-related merger in 2017, Dena–Vijaya with Bank of Baroda in 2019, and Andhra–Corporation and Allahabad Bank mergers in 2020.
The expected gains included scale, lower costs, global-size lenders, better capital use and improved risk management.
Narasimham-II recommended consolidation through mergers of strong banks and the creation of fewer, stronger banking institutions.

secs.t: PSB reform agenda - EASE Reforms and Index, Indradhanush, Banks Board Bureau, recapitalisation bonds

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2024 - the statement that EASE is "governed by a board of heads of premier FIs" is
false
; IBA's steering committee runs it.
The seven components were Appointments, Banks Board Bureau, Capitalisation, De-stressing, Empowerment, Framework of accountability and Governance.
Indradhanush was introduced in August 2015, included the Banks Board Bureau, and provided ₹70,000 crore of budgetary capital over four years.
Under the mechanism, the Government issues bonds to public sector banks and puts the money back into them as equity; therefore, no equivalent fresh cash leaves the budget immediately.
Quarterly benchmarking of mid-size and large public sector banks against reform themes provides the basis for ranking them in the EASE Index.
EASE uses quarterly reporting, its earlier versions covered the listed reform themes, and EASE 5.0–7.0 formed EASENext after PSB Manthan 2.0 in April 2022.
EASE aims include financial stability, credit growth, NPA management, risk mitigation, digital transformation, customer service and inclusion.
The record combined net profit of ₹1.98 lakh crore in FY26 was cited as meaning that budgetary recapitalisation is not currently needed.

secs.t: Financial sector reforms after 1991 - components

x: The SLR was
38.5 per cent
in 1991–92 and was subsequently reduced along with reductions in reserve requirements.
Post-1991 reforms introduced prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, along with CRAR in 1992.
SEBI became statutory in 1992, the market-determined exchange rate was introduced in 1993, FEMA replaced FERA in 1999, and insurance was opened under the IRDA Act in 1999.

secs.t: RRB consolidation - amalgamation rounds, One State One RRB

x: There were originally 196 RRBs, and their number came down to 43 after the 2020–21 consolidation.
Under the One State-One RRB arrangement, 15 RRBs were amalgamated and the number became 28, effective from 1 May 2025.
Viability Plan 2.0 covers all 28 RRBs, rests on four pillars and tracks 30 parameters.

secs.t: Privatisation debate - IDBI Bank, Banking Laws Amendment, PSB privatisation

x: Following LIC’s acquisition of a majority stake in 2019, RBI reclassified IDBI Bank as a private sector lender.
The Government and LIC proposed the sale of a combined
strategic stake in IDBI Bank.
The Act came into force on 1 August 2025 and made 19 amendments across the RBI Act, Banking Regulation Act, SBI Act, and the Banking Companies Acts of 1970 and 1980.

secs.t: Deposit insurance - DICGC status and cover limit

x: The deposit insurance limit was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in the
Budget, following the PMC Bank crisis.
DICGC covers commercial banks, including foreign bank branches, regional rural banks and cooperative banks, but excludes deposits of foreign, Central and State governments.
Deposits accepted by NBFCs are not covered by DICGC, whereas the other listed banking institutions fall within the covered categories.

secs.t: Basel Accords vs Basel Convention - body and subject

x: The Basel Convention on hazardous wastes was adopted in 1989 and entered into force in 1992.
The Basel Accords are associated with the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), based in Basel, Switzerland.
The Basel Convention is an environmental treaty dealing with the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes and their disposal.

secs.t: Governance of PSBs - Banks Board Bureau, P.J. Nayak, privatisation

x: The Banks Board Bureau originated from the
Indradhanush
initiative and began functioning in 2016.
The
Financial Services Institutions Bureau
(FSIB) replaced the Banks Board Bureau in 2022.
The debate balances possible gains in efficiency and governance against the social mandate of public sector banks, including rural branches and priority lending.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Budget 2026–27 announced the High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat and restructuring of PFC and REC.
Bank mergers can involve significant
integration costs
, including the task of combining systems, personnel and operations.
The draft proposed lower differentiated risk weights for
MSMEs and real estate
, which would reduce minimum capital needs.
The expected credit loss shift was estimated to reduce Tier-1 ratios by about
100–150 basis points

rows.title: Non-performing assets - causes, twin balance sheet problem, recognition and provisioning

secs.t: NPA definition - overdue period, classification (standard, sub-standard, doubtful, loss)

x: A loan or advance becomes an NPA when interest or principal is overdue for more than
90 days
Agricultural loans become NPAs after two crop seasons for short-duration crops or one crop season for long-duration crops.
SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2 cover 1–30, 31–60 and 61–90 overdue days respectively.
An asset is classified as
doubtful
when it has remained substandard for more than 12 months.

secs.t: Stress indicators - interest coverage ratio, SMA-0/1/2, restructured and stressed assets

x: SMA-0 covers 0–30 days, SMA-1 covers 31–60 days, SMA-2 covers 61–90 days, and an NPA is generally beyond 90 days overdue.
The sequence proceeds from SMA-0 to SMA-1 and SMA-2, followed by NPA classification as sub-standard, doubtful and loss.
Interest Coverage Ratio equals operating earnings, or EBIT, divided by interest due.

secs.t: Gross NPA vs net NPA - trend and peak year, PSB vs private banks

x: Net NPA is calculated as Gross NPA minus
provisions
SCB GNPA peaked at approximately 11.2 per cent in
March 2018
, after the Asset Quality Review.
In March 2026, GNPA was 1.93 per cent and NNPA was 0.39 per cent, described as a decadal low.
The reported June 2026 GNPA figures were HDFC 1.17 per cent, ICICI 1.38 per cent and Axis 1.28 per cent.

secs.t: Provisioning coverage ratio and income recognition norms

x: PCR is the ratio of provisions held to Gross NPAs.
The reported SCB PCR for March 2025 was
76.3 per cent
IRACP means
Income Recognition, Asset Classification, Provisioning
Stage 1 involves 12-month expected loss, Stage 2 lifetime loss, Stage 3 full lifetime provision, and loss allowances use the effective interest rate method.

secs.t: Twin balance sheet problem - meaning, which Economic Survey framed it

x: The twin balance sheet problem describes over-leveraged firms alongside capital-starved banks burdened with NPAs.
The Economic Survey
, under Chief Economic Adviser Arvind Subramanian, discussed the festering twin balance sheet problem.
Over-leveraged firms face difficulty investing.

secs.t: Causes of NPAs - infrastructure lending, evergreening, wilful defaulters

x: Evergreening involves extending fresh loans to repay old loans, thereby keeping the underlying default hidden.
The Asset Quality Review exposed hidden stress and ended the practice of keeping defaults concealed through evergreening.
Aggressive lending and shocks lead to NPAs, which require provisioning and cause capital erosion, resulting in weak credit growth.

secs.t: Asset Quality Review - year, purpose, outcome

x: The AQR was designed to uncover hidden NPAs and ensure that banks recognised the underlying asset quality problems.
The 2015 AQR required recognition of hidden stressed loans, caused reported NPAs to rise sharply, made the problem transparent and contributed to subsequent IBC and recapitalisation measures.
The AQR brought hidden stressed loans onto bank books, resulting in a sharp increase in reported NPAs and greater transparency.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: SCB credit nearly tripled from
₹67 lakh crore in 2015 to ₹181 lakh crore in 2025
, alongside the cleaning up of bank balance sheets.
A key criticism of the ECL approach is that
it raises the capital needs of banks
Only
about 13%
of written-off loans were recovered, indicating that low NPAs are partly explained by write-offs rather than complete recovery.

rows.title: NPA resolution - SARFAESI, DRTs, IBC 2016, NARCL/bad bank, Prompt Corrective Action framework
sub: Group-II M2-A-26: Non-performing assets - causes, resolution mechanisms (SARFAESI, IBC, NARCL) and PCA

secs.t: Prompt Corrective Action framework - full form, trigger parameters, restrictions

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2019 asked the expansion "PCA = Prompt Corrective Action".
PCA stands for
Prompt Corrective Action
, a framework used by the Reserve Bank of India to intervene in banks with weakening financial health.
The current PCA triggers are capital, measured through CRAR and CET1, asset quality measured through net NPA, and leverage measured through the Tier-1 leverage ratio.

secs.t: Earlier resolution mechanisms - CDR, SDR, S4A, 5/25, Project Sashakt ICA, Prudential Framework

x: SDR, introduced in 2015, allowed lenders to
convert debt into a majority equity stake of 51 per cent or more and change the management
of the borrowing company.
The Prudential Framework requires a 30-day review after default, makes the Inter-Creditor Agreement mandatory and envisages resolution within 180 days.
Under the stated SARFAESI provision, lenders holding
75 per cent
of the dues issue a 60-day notice under Section 13(2).

secs.t: IBC 2016 - insolvency vs bankruptcy, CIRP timelines, NCLT/NCLAT, IBBI, CoC, pre-packs for MSMEs

x: NCLAT hears appeals from the NCLT, IBBI, CCI and NFRA under the specified provisions and dates.
Appeals from the NCLT lie to the NCLAT, and a further appeal lies to the Supreme Court.
The IBC replaced fragmented provisions with a single, time-bound, creditor-in-control insolvency process.
Section 29A
prevents wilful defaulters and promoters of NPAs from submitting resolution bids, subject to the statutory framework.
The IBC replaced the earlier scattered framework, including the Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1985 and the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction.
CIRP ordinarily has a 180-day period with an extension and an outer limit of 330 days including litigation.
Resolution costs, workmen’s dues and secured creditors
rank above government dues in the stated liquidation waterfall.
Wilful defaulters and NPA promoters are barred from bidding for their own firms.
NCLT and NCLAT were constituted on
1 June 2016
under Sections 408 and 410 of the Companies Act, 2013.
IBBI regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies and information utilities.
The 2026 amendment requires the NCLT to admit or reject a CIRP plea within
14 days

secs.t: SARFAESI Act 2002 - ARCs, enforcement without courts

x: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 was based on the
Narasimham Committee
SARFAESI permits banks to enforce security over NPAs without prior court intervention, subject to the statutory safeguards and remedies.
Under Section 13(8), the borrower can redeem the secured asset only until publication of the auction notice.

secs.t: Debt Recovery Tribunals - threshold and appellate tribunal

x: DRTs were established under the
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
, and are also used under SARFAESI.
The DRTs and DRATs handle debts above
₹20 lakh
under the stated framework.
The FY 2024 shares were IBC 48%, SARFAESI 32%, DRTs 17% and Lok Adalats 3%.

secs.t: Lok Adalats for small NPAs

x: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under
the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
Lok Adalats provide quick, fee-free settlement through compromise between the parties.
Lok Adalats settle only small NPAs and account for about
3 per cent
of recoveries.
The DRT Visakhapatnam bench settled 13 cases valued at ₹46.11 crore on 13 September 2026.

secs.t: NARCL and IDRCL - bad bank structure, ownership, funding, guarantee

x: NARCL aggregates large stressed loans, while IDRCL manages their resolution, including sale to AIFs.
The Government guarantees NARCL’s Security Receipts up to
₹30,600 crore for five years or until settlement
, whichever is relevant.
By 30 June 2025, NARCL had acquired 27 accounts with ₹1,57,215 crore exposure and recovered ₹2,410 crore.

secs.t: Stress indicators and causes - ICR, twin balance sheet, evergreening, over-leverage

x: ICR is
EBIT divided by interest payable
and measures the firm’s capacity to service interest.
Evergreening occurs when fresh loans are used to repay old loans, thereby concealing the underlying NPA.
The Asset Quality Review exposed evergreening and other hidden stressed loans that had not been properly recognised.
Loan frauds, diversion of funds, weak credit appraisal, slow recovery and corporate over-leverage are causes of stress.

secs.t: Gross vs net NPA, PCR - latest trend (FSR)

x: A higher PCR means a larger proportion of Gross NPAs is covered by provisions, making the bank more resilient.
For March 2025, the reported figures were
GNPA 2.3%, NNPA 0.5%, PCR 76.3%, CRAR 17.3% and CET1 14.7%
The indicated changes are a move to Expected Credit Loss provisioning and higher risk weights for unsecured consumer credit and NBFC exposures.

secs.t: Wilful defaulters and fraud reporting

x: Wilful defaulters are
barred from bidding
under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
Personal guarantors remain liable even after approval of a resolution plan, as affirmed in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India (2021).
The number of suspicious transaction reports received by FIU-IND was reported to have increased by
45 per cent

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The NCLT bench sits at Amaravati, while the DRT Visakhapatnam bench settles cases at Lok Adalats; statement 3 confuses their locations.
The correct comparison is that SARFAESI enables secured lenders to proceed without court intervention, IBC is collective and NCLT-led, and DRT provides tribunal-based recovery.
The Finance Minister described the IBC as “not a debt-recovery tool”; its principal emphasis is insolvency resolution and value realisation rather than ordinary debt recovery.

rows.title: Financial inclusion - PMJDY, MUDRA, microfinance and SHG-bank linkage; digital payments and UPI
sub: Group-II M2-A-27: Financial inclusion and digital finance - PMJDY, MUDRA, UPI and the JAM trinity

secs.t: PMJDY - launch, objective, features, accounts and deposits

x: Exam angle: "Which 2014 reform aimed at banking access for all households?" - PMJDY.
The
Nachiket Mor Committee
, constituted in 2013, laid the groundwork for these features of universal financial access.
PMJDY provides zero-balance basic savings accounts with interest, RuPay debit cards and DBT functionality.
PMJDY accounts are linked with the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana and Atal Pension Yojana.
The reported figures were
45.95 crore rural/semi-urban accounts and 32.92 crore women account holders

secs.t: Payment systems and NPCI products - purpose, UPI abroad

x: UPI links multiple bank accounts in one application, supports P2P and P2M payments, and operates 24x7.
UPI 2.0 included overdraft linking, mandates, invoice checking, signed QR and a ₹2 lakh per-day limit; it did not impose a mandatory minimum transaction value.
e-RUPI is a
person- and purpose-specific prepaid digital voucher
and was used in 13 government schemes.
RTGS settles transactions individually in real time on a gross basis, while NEFT uses deferred net settlement in half-hourly batches.
Zero MDR on RuPay debit and BHIM-UPI transactions applied from
1 January 2020
The reported international UPI network covered 11 countries in 2026, including Cambodia through KHQR and countries such as Greece and Maldives.
Cambodia through KHQR, Greece, Maldives and Qatar were all included among the reported UPI international destinations.
The later amendment allows a small MDR on some high-value transactions, while UPI remains free for consumers.

secs.t: Digital payments indices - base year, parameters, frequency; progress

x: Exam angle: "DPI base year 2021" is the classic wrong statement - base is March 2018.
The five RBI-DPI parameters are payment enablers, payment infrastructure on the demand side, payment infrastructure on the supply side, payment performance and consumer centricity.
Payment enablers correspond to factors enabling payments; demand-side infrastructure is user-side, supply-side infrastructure is provider-side, and consumer centricity is consumer-oriented.
The Department of Financial Services runs the scheme, which provides 0.15% for eligible BHIM-UPI P2M payments up to ₹2,000, with NPCI as nodal agency.
All four statements correctly describe UPI's international presence, the Singapore remittance linkage, Cambodia's KHQR arrangement and NIPL's wider partnerships.
Despite widespread UPI use, over 90% of UPI users still use cash, making payment behaviour hybrid rather than exclusively digital.
The incentive was
for BHIM-UPI person-to-merchant transactions up to ₹2,000, with DFS as the scheme authority and NPCI as nodal body.

secs.t: Crypto and digital currency - crypto vs payment apps, Digital Rupee vs UPI, ONDC

x: The e₹ is RBI liability and legal tender, whereas UPI transfers bank-account money and is associated with bank-deposit liability.
DEA and RBI are working on interlinking central bank digital currencies to support
cross-border payments
ONDC seeks to create an open digital commerce network and break e-commerce platform monopolies.
ONDC is identified as part of India Stack along with Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and Account Aggregator.
The stated benefits include programmability, targeted subsidy delivery, cheaper remittances and traceability for tax compliance.

secs.t: MUDRA - ministry, categories, limits, refinance

x: MUDRA Ltd was set up as a subsidiary of
SIDBI
on 18 March 2015 and undertakes refinance functions.
PMMY covers non-corporate, non-farm micro and small enterprises in manufacturing, trading, services and allied agricultural activities.
The later CDI figure refers to more than 57 crore loans worth about ₹40 lakh crore, with 66% of loans going to women and nearly half to SC, ST and OBC borrowers.

secs.t: Financial inclusion and digital payment committees

x: Rangarajan dealt with financial inclusion; Watal with digital payments; Mohanty with the medium-term path on financial inclusion; and Malegam with the microfinance sector after the AP crisis.
The FI-Index covers 97 indicators relating to banking, investment, insurance, postal and pension services; its scale is 0–100 and it is published every July.

secs.t: SHG-bank linkage - pilot, institutions, NRLM, AP SERP/DWCRA

x: DAY-NRLM is associated with more than 90.90 lakh SHGs, 10.05 crore rural women households and a repayment rate exceeding 98%.
The Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA) programme in Andhra Pradesh dates to
and preceded the present SHG model.
The reported SERP structure includes 8.50 lakh SHGs, 89.21 lakh women, 27,422 Village Organisations, 660 Mandal Samakhyas and 26 Zilla Samakhyas.

secs.t: Social security trio - PMJJBY, PMSBY, APY

x: APY replaced Swavalamban, provides a monthly pension of ₹1,000–₹5,000 from age 60, is administered by PFRDA, and excludes taxpayers from new enrolment from 1 October 2022.
PMJJBY, PMSBY and APY were launched together on 9 May 2015; therefore, the schemes have the same launch date and the listed order is the valid sequence among the options.
The cited CDI enrolment figures are 27.33 crore for PMJJBY, 57.92 crore for PMSBY and 8.96 crore for APY.

secs.t: New digital finance architecture - payments banks, AA, ONDC, OCEN

x: Account Aggregators can speed up credit appraisal by allowing lenders to access bank transaction and GST data with the borrower's consent.
OCEN, or Open Credit Enablement Network, provides common protocols connecting lenders and marketplaces for small-ticket credit.

Both statements are true, and consent-based access to relevant financial data through Account Aggregators directly explains how digital architecture can improve credit appraisal for first-time borrowers.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct: the 2026 Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha, permits the Centre to modify zero-MDR, and allows the possibility of MDR on high-value UPI payments while retaining free consumer access.

All four statements describe the reported significance of UPI: verifiable transaction histories, credit growth without higher defaults, association with higher output, and 45% of transactions from Tier-2 and smaller cities.

rows.title: Financial markets - money market instruments and capital market segments

secs.t: Gilt-edged market and government securities - G-Secs, SDLs, T-bills, primary dealers, RBI Retail Direct

x: Exam angle: "Gilt-edged market deals with" - government securities, not corporate paper.
Treasury Bills do not carry periodic interest and are issued at a discount; Cash Management Bills address temporary cash mismatches; and SDLs are long-term State Government borrowings.
RBI Retail Direct
enables individuals to buy Government securities directly through a Retail Direct Gilt, or RDG, account.

secs.t: Money market instruments - maturity and issuer; money vs capital market

x: Commercial Paper is an unsecured short-term promissory instrument issued by eligible corporates.
The current RBI maturity range stated for Commercial Paper is
seven days to one year
TREPS, or the tri-party repo arrangement, replaced
CBLO
The regulatory statement is reversed: the money market is regulated by RBI and the capital market by SEBI.
The money market is not confined to equity shares; equity is a capital-market instrument.

secs.t: Capital market segments and instruments - equity, debt, VC, PE, ETFs

x: The capital-market structure includes
development financial institutions such as IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, SIDBI and UTI
, in addition to other segments and intermediaries.
Convertible preference share
s and partly or optionally convertible debentures are hybrid instruments.
An ETF is traded on a stock exchange and its market price generally remains close to its net asset value.

secs.t: Bond types and bond yield drivers

x: The Sovereign Gold Bond was launched in 2015 and offered 2.5% interest along with returns linked to the price of gold.
Bond prices and yields generally move inversely: when the market price of an existing bond falls, its yield rises, and vice versa.
RBI purchases through OMOs and foreign inflows increase demand for Government bonds, supporting prices and generally lowering yields.

secs.t: Alternative investment funds - categories, REITs and InvITs

x: Category I AIFs include venture capital, angel, SME, social venture and infrastructure funds.
Category III AIFs include hedge funds, may use leveraged trading and are allowed in commodity derivatives.
Alternative Investment Funds are privately pooled vehicles regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India.
REITs and InvITs pool income-yielding real-estate or infrastructure assets and facilitate asset monetisation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Budget 2026–27 framework included market-making for corporate bonds, derivatives on corporate bond indices and measures supporting bigger municipal bonds.
Andhra Pradesh planned open market borrowings through SDLs of
₹73,383 crore
